evidence.snippet: We evaluated the safety and efficacy of an investigational RNA interference therapeutic, fazirsiran, that degrades Z-AAT messenger RNA, reducing deleterious protein synthesis.
evidence.explanation: The Phase 2 report states the RNA-interference mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Fazirsiran reduced serum and liver concentrations of Z-AAT in a dose-dependent manner and reduced hepatic globule burden.
evidence.explanation: SEQUOIA Phase 2 RCT establishes fazirsiran as a liver-targeted siRNA that addresses the gain-of-toxic-function arm of AATD by lowering hepatic Z-AAT.

evidence.snippet: All fazirsiran-treated patients had histologic reduction from baseline in hepatic globule burden.
evidence.explanation: Histologic endpoint confirms target engagement at the hepatocyte level, the proximal pathologic lesion of AATD liver disease.

treatments/8.description: The RNA-interference therapeutic fazirsiran degrades Z-AAT mRNA. In the Phase 2 SEQUOIA trial, it produced dose-dependent serum and liver Z-AAT reduction and reduced hepatic globule burden.

treatments/8/targets/0.description: SERPINA1 mRNA silencing reduces synthesis and hepatic accumulation of Z-AAT.

evidence.snippet: Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for severe disease (will restore AAT levels).
evidence.explanation: Establishes liver transplantation as definitive curative treatment that restores normal AAT production from donor liver

evidence.snippet: Rarely, patients require liver transplant and typically the patient outcomes are excellent.
evidence.explanation: Documents excellent outcomes in AAT deficiency patients undergoing liver transplantation

evidence.snippet: Pi∗ZZ individuals harbor an up to 20 times higher risk of liver fibrosis and cirrhosis than noncarriers and liver transplantation is currently the only available therapeutic option.
evidence.explanation: Confirms liver transplantation as essential therapeutic option for severe ZZ genotype liver disease

evidence.snippet: Our case provides initial evidence that A1ATD heterozygote donors may be safely used for pediatric patients with A1ATD, thus expanding the donor pool.
evidence.explanation: Documents that heterozygous donors can be successfully used for AAT deficiency recipients, expanding available donor options

treatments/9.description: Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for severe AATD liver disease and restores circulating AAT levels.

treatments/9/targets/0.description: A donor liver replaces hepatocytes that synthesize and retain pathogenic Z-AAT.

evidence.snippet: Evidence regarding management is limited to case reports and small case series.
evidence.explanation: The systematic review documents the limited evidence base for this rare manifestation.

open_questions/0.rationale: Human biopsy establishes the lesion, but the cached disease-specific evidence does not justify a more specific protease-causal edge.

evidence.snippet: Since not all patients with the same homozygous PIZZ genotype develop end-stage disease, it is hypothesized that there is likely to be a strong influence of genetic and environmental modifiers of the injury cascade and of the fibrotic response.
evidence.explanation: The review explicitly identifies unexplained modifier effects on liver-disease progression.

open_questions/1.rationale: Variable progression limits individual risk prediction and stratification for liver-directed therapy.

evidence.snippet: It has been unclear whether PI*Z AAT elicits liver cell UPR, due in part to limitations of current cellular and animal models.
evidence.explanation: The study explicitly motivates new models because existing cellular and animal systems are limited.

open_questions/2.rationale: Current models clarify hepatocyte UPR biology but do not establish that one system recapitulates both target organs or human clinical variability.

evidence.snippet: Anal cancer, caused by persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV), is rare in the general population.
evidence.explanation: Supports persistent oncogenic HPV infection as the necessary causal environmental exposure for anal cancer.

evidence.snippet: certain groups, such as men who have sex with men living with HIV, are at much higher risk
evidence.explanation: Supports HIV infection (particularly in MSM) as a major risk modifier for anal cancer.

evidence.snippet: Current smokers among men and women were at particularly high risk for anal cancer, independent of age and other risk factors
evidence.explanation: Population-based case-control study supports current cigarette smoking as an independent risk factor for anal cancer in both men and women, independent of HPV-related sexual exposures.

evidence.snippet: receptive anal intercourse was related strongly to the risk of anal cancer
evidence.explanation: Population-based case-control study supports a history of receptive anal intercourse as a strong sexual-behavior risk factor for anal cancer, consistent with its role in anogenital HPV acquisition.

evidence.snippet: HPV was positive in 85% of the SCC cases, with HPV-16 as the most prevalent genotype
evidence.explanation: Registry data document a high HPV prevalence in anal canal SCC with HPV-16 as the most common genotype, supporting HPV infection of anal squamous epithelium as the upstream pathophysiologic step.

steps/4.description: High-risk HPV (predominantly HPV-16) infects basal stratified squamous epithelial cells of the anal canal, typically at the anal transformation zone where squamous and columnar epithelia meet. Persistent infection over years to decades is the necessary first step in HPV-driven anal carcinogenesis.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that the E6 proteins of the oncogenic HPVs that bind p53 stimulate the degradation of p53.
evidence.explanation: Classic biochemical evidence that HPV E6 from oncogenic types stimulates degradation of p53, supporting E6-mediated p53 loss as a shared mechanism in HPV-driven anogenital cancers including anal squamous cell carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: p53 is ATP dependent and involves the ubiquitin-dependent protease system.
evidence.explanation: E6-promoted p53 degradation occurs via the ubiquitin-proteasome system, providing direct mechanistic support for proteasomal destruction of p53 in HPV-infected squamous epithelium.

steps/5.description: The HPV E6 oncoprotein binds to the cellular E3 ubiquitin ligase E6AP and targets p53 for proteasomal degradation. Loss of p53 function eliminates DNA damage checkpoints and apoptotic responses in infected anal squamous epithelial cells.

evidence.snippet: the E7 oncoprotein of the human papilloma virus type-16 can form similar complexes with p105-RB.
evidence.explanation: Classic biochemical evidence that HPV-16 E7 binds the retinoblastoma gene product, supporting E7-mediated pRB inactivation as the shared mechanism driving uncontrolled S-phase entry in HPV-driven anogenital carcinomas, including anal squamous cell carcinoma.

steps/6.description: The HPV E7 oncoprotein binds to and inactivates the retinoblastoma protein (pRB), releasing E2F transcription factors and driving uncontrolled cell cycle progression in anal squamous epithelial cells.

evidence.snippet: The most frequently mutated genes included PIK3CA (28.1%), KMT2D (19.5%), FBXW7 (12%), TP53 (12%) and PTEN (10.8%).
evidence.explanation: Multiplatform molecular profiling of 311 anal squamous cell carcinomas identifies recurrent somatic mutations across PIK3CA, KMT2D, FBXW7, TP53, and PTEN, supporting genomic instability and accumulation of driver alterations during anal squamous cell carcinogenesis.

steps/7.description: Combined loss of p53 and pRB function, along with HPV-associated chromosomal aberrations, drives accumulation of genetic alterations and progression from anal intraepithelial neoplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: the benefits of treating precancerous anal lesions to reduce the risk of progression to anal SCC
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of anal cancer screening recommendations supports the AIN-to-invasive-SCC progression pathway as the rationale for treating high-grade precancerous anal lesions in high-risk groups.

steps/8.description: HPV-driven dysplasia of the anal squamous epithelium progresses through a spectrum of anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN1, AIN2, AIN3 / high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion) to invasive anal squamous cell carcinoma. High-grade lesions carry a significant risk of progression, particularly in immunosuppressed patients.

evidence.snippet: The expression of PD-1 was seen in 68.8% and PD-L1 in 40.5% of tumors.
evidence.explanation: Multiplatform profiling of 311 anal squamous cell carcinomas documents PD-L1 expression in 40.5% of tumors and PD-1 expression on infiltrating cells in 68.8%, supporting adaptive immune resistance as an active mechanism in anal squamous cell carcinoma and providing the rationale for PD-1 checkpoint blockade.

steps/9.description: Anal squamous cell carcinoma cells frequently express PD-L1 and PD-1 is expressed on tumor-infiltrating T cells, consistent with adaptive immune resistance to anti-tumor immunity. This mechanism is the therapeutic rationale for PD-1 blockade (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) in recurrent or metastatic disease.

evidence.snippet: Hematochezia is the passage of frank blood per rectum
evidence.explanation: Reference clinical definition of hematochezia as bright red bleeding per rectum, which is the most common presenting symptom of anal canal cancer.

evidence.snippet: common presenting symptom is bleeding, with up to one third of patients
evidence.explanation: This anal SCC review supports bleeding as the most common presenting symptom of anal canal squamous carcinoma.

steps/10.description: Bright red bleeding per rectum is the most common presenting symptom of anal canal cancer and frequently prompts initial evaluation.

evidence.snippet: Patients diagnosed with both cancers often experience multiple symptoms including pain, constipation, nausea, and vomiting.
evidence.explanation: Palliative care review of colorectal and anal malignancies supports pain as a common symptom experienced by patients with anal cancer.

steps/11.description: Pain is among the multiple symptoms commonly experienced by patients with anal canal cancer over the course of their disease, as documented in palliative care studies of colorectal and anal malignancies.

evidence.snippet: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal (SCCA) is an uncommon malignancy with limited therapeutic options.
evidence.explanation: Supports anal canal squamous cell carcinoma as the defining neoplastic entity of HPV-associated anal canal cancer.

steps/12.description: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal is the defining histopathologic feature of HPV-associated anal canal cancer.

evidence.snippet: Primary tumor progression was associated with metastasis and recurrence of the inguinal node
evidence.explanation: Multicenter cohort of 435 patients with anal canal squamous cell carcinoma supports inguinal lymph node metastasis as a key pattern of regional spread, consistent with the lymphatic drainage of the anal canal below the dentate line.

steps/13.description: Anal canal cancer below the dentate line drains preferentially to inguinal lymph nodes; palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy may indicate regional metastatic involvement.

edges/0.description: Persistent HPV infection enables sustained E6 expression

edges/1.description: Persistent HPV infection enables sustained E7 expression

edges/2.description: p53 loss permits cells with damaged DNA to survive and proliferate

edges/3.description: Unrestrained proliferation in the setting of impaired checkpoints

edges/4.description: Genomic alterations drive progression from AIN to invasive carcinoma

edges/5.description: Invasive HPV-driven anal squamous cell carcinoma upregulates PD-L1 and engages adaptive immune resistance to evade anti-tumor T cell responses.

evidence.snippet: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal (SCCA) is an uncommon malignancy with limited therapeutic options.
evidence.explanation: The anal SCC profiling cohort directly identifies squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal as the invasive neoplastic entity.

edges/6.description: HPV-driven dysplasia progression culminates in invasive anal canal squamous carcinoma, the defining neoplastic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: common presenting symptom is bleeding, with up to one third of patients
evidence.explanation: The anal SCC review supports bleeding as the most common presenting symptom of anal canal squamous carcinoma.

edges/7.description: Invasive anal canal squamous carcinoma commonly presents with bleeding.

evidence.snippet: Patients diagnosed with both cancers often experience multiple symptoms including pain, constipation, nausea, and vomiting.
evidence.explanation: The palliative care review supports pain among symptoms experienced by patients with anal malignancies.

edges/8.description: Anal canal cancer can produce anal or perirectal pain as a local symptom.

evidence.snippet: Primary tumor progression was associated with metastasis and recurrence of the inguinal node
evidence.explanation: The multicenter cohort supports inguinal node involvement as a pattern of anal canal squamous carcinoma progression.

edges/9.description: Primary tumor progression can involve inguinal nodes, producing inguinal lymphadenopathy.

evidence.snippet: Anal cancer, caused by persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV), is rare in the general population.
evidence.explanation: States that anal cancer is caused by persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus, the infection this node represents.

edges/10.description: Persistent high-risk HPV is the necessary cause of this cancer, and the entry models the infection itself as the initiating node, so this link is an identity rather than a causal step.

evidence.snippet: certain groups, such as men who have sex with men living with HIV, are at much higher risk
evidence.explanation: Reports much higher risk among men who have sex with men living with HIV, the group in whom impaired clearance permits persistent infection.

edges/11.description: Immunosuppression does not cause the infection; it prevents its clearance, converting transient HPV into the persistent infection this node requires. That is why risk concentrates so sharply in people living with HIV.

evidence.snippet: Current smokers among men and women were at particularly high risk for anal cancer, independent of age and other risk factors
evidence.explanation: Reports current smokers at particularly high risk for anal cancer independent of age and other factors, an effect separate from viral acquisition.

edges/12.description: Smoking raises risk independently of HPV exposure and sexual behaviour, so it targets progression of established neoplasia rather than acquisition of the virus. No mediating step is identified in the cited study.

evidence.snippet: receptive anal intercourse was related strongly to the risk of anal cancer
evidence.explanation: Reports receptive anal intercourse as strongly related to anal cancer risk, the transmission route that delivers the virus to this epithelium.

edges/13.description: Not a carcinogen but the route of acquisition: it is how the virus reaches anal squamous epithelium in the first place, with sexual transmission as the known intervening step.

evidence.snippet: Human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative tumors are frequently TP53-mutated (TP53-MT) and often resistant to therapy.
evidence.explanation: Multiplatform profiling of 311 anal SCC specimens supports the pattern of TP53 mutation enrichment in HPV-negative anal squamous cell carcinoma, distinct from the HPV-driven E6-mediated p53 degradation seen in HPV-positive disease.

genes/0.notes: In HPV-positive anal squamous cell carcinoma, p53 function is lost through E6-mediated degradation rather than somatic TP53 mutation. Rare HPV-negative anal cancers may harbor TP53 mutations.

evidence.snippet: The most frequently mutated genes included PIK3CA (28.1%)
evidence.explanation: Large molecular profiling cohort supports PIK3CA as the most frequently mutated gene in anal canal squamous cell carcinoma.

genes/1.notes: Somatic PIK3CA mutations occur in approximately a quarter of anal squamous cell carcinomas and may represent a therapeutic target via PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling.

evidence.snippet: All cases in this sample could potentially have been prevented by nonavalent prophylactic vaccination, and 97% by the quadrivalent vaccine.
evidence.explanation: Lesion-specific HPV genotyping of anal squamous cell carcinomas in women indicates that nonavalent (and largely quadrivalent) HPV vaccination could prevent the great majority of HPV-driven anal cancers, supporting HPV vaccination as primary prevention.

treatments/0.description: Prophylactic vaccination against high-risk HPV types prevents anogenital HPV infection and reduces the incidence of anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and anal cancer. Most effective when given before HPV exposure.

evidence.snippet: Since the original contribution by Nigro in 1974, surprisingly few changes have been made to the standard of care in chemotherapy, which still consists of a combination of 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin C.
evidence.explanation: Establishes 5-fluorouracil plus mitomycin C combined with radiation (the Nigro regimen) as the long-standing standard chemoradiation backbone for anal canal cancer.

evidence.snippet: The adoption of chemoradiotherapy (CRT) increased from 14% in the 1990 s to over 80% after 2010, achieving survival outcomes comparable to surgery.
evidence.explanation: Registry data document the shift from primary surgery to chemoradiation as the dominant curative treatment for anal canal carcinoma, supporting its role as standard curative therapy.

treatments/1.description: Concurrent 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin-C with external-beam radiation therapy is the standard curative treatment for localized anal canal squamous cell carcinoma, preserving anal sphincter function and avoiding upfront abdominoperineal resection.

evidence.snippet: The primary treatment for locoregional failure following chemoradiotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma of the anus (SCCA) is salvage abdominoperineal resection (APR).
evidence.explanation: Multicenter retrospective cohort supports salvage abdominoperineal resection as the standard treatment for locoregional failure after definitive chemoradiation for anal squamous cell carcinoma.

treatments/2.description: Surgical removal of the anus, rectum, and surrounding tissues with permanent colostomy is reserved for residual or recurrent anal canal carcinoma after definitive chemoradiation.

evidence.snippet: Pembrolizumab monotherapy is a possible treatment option with a favourable benefit-risk ratio for patients with previously treated advanced anal squamous cell carcinoma who have no alternative satisfactory treatment options.
evidence.explanation: Phase 2 KEYNOTE-158 cohort supports pembrolizumab as an active second-line treatment for advanced anal squamous cell carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: 12 (11%, 95% CI 6-18) patients had an objective response, including 11 (15%, 8-25) of 75 patients with PD-L1-positive tumours and one (3%; 0-17) of 30 patients with PD-L1-negative tumours.
evidence.explanation: KEYNOTE-158 quantifies pembrolizumab activity in previously treated advanced anal squamous cell carcinoma (objective response in 11% of 112 patients), with responses enriched in PD-L1-positive tumours (15% vs 3%), consistent with adaptive immune resistance as the targeted mechanism.

treatments/3.description: PD-1 inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab have demonstrated activity in recurrent or metastatic anal canal squamous cell carcinoma and are used in the second-line and beyond setting.

evidence.snippet: Pembrolizumab monotherapy is a possible treatment option with a favourable benefit-risk ratio for patients with previously treated advanced anal squamous cell carcinoma who have no alternative satisfactory treatment options.
evidence.explanation: Clinical activity of pembrolizumab in advanced anal squamous cell carcinoma supports targeting PD-1-mediated adaptive immune resistance as a therapeutically relevant mechanism.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: PD-1 blockade with pembrolizumab counteracts adaptive immune resistance by interrupting PD-1/PD-L1 signaling between tumor-infiltrating T cells and PD-L1-expressing anal squamous cell carcinoma cells, restoring anti-tumor T cell activity.

evidence.snippet: the disease is caused by mutations in SMAD3. This gene encodes a member of the TGF-β pathway that is essential for TGF-β signal transmission
evidence.explanation: van de Laar et al. identified SMAD3 as the causal gene, encoding an essential mediator of TGF-beta signal transmission.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous loss-of-function SMAD3 (Mothers against decapentaplegic homolog 3) mutations lead to aneurysm-osteoarthritis syndrome (AOS).
evidence.explanation: States the established human genetic mechanism; the paper then models it in Smad3-deficient mice and reports a further patient family.

steps/1.description: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in SMAD3 disrupt the receptor-regulated SMAD that transduces TGF-beta signals from activated TGF-beta receptors to the nucleus. SMAD3 forms a complex with the co-SMAD SMAD4 and regulates transcription of TGF-beta target genes. Loss of normal SMAD3 function is the conserved genetic trigger for the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: RNA sequencing of Loeys-Dietz syndrome 3 SMCs revealed reduced microfibril gene expression.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived aortic SMC transcriptomics directly supports reduced microfibril-gene expression.

evidence.snippet: SMAD3 overexpression rescued both PRRX2 and microfibril expression.
evidence.explanation: Rescue by SMAD3 overexpression directly supports the direction of the SMAD3-PRRX2-microfibril regulatory relationship in patient-derived cells.

steps/2.description: In a multigenerational SMAD3 p.Arg287Gln family, aortic smooth muscle cells showed reduced expression of microfibril genes and downregulation of PRRX2, a promoter-occupying regulator of five microfibril genes. SMAD3 overexpression rescued both PRRX2 and microfibril expression, defining a directly tested SMAD3-PRRX2-microfibril axis.

evidence.snippet: SMAD3 mutations lead to increased aortic expression of several key players in the TGF-β pathway, including SMAD3
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates paradoxically increased aortic TGF-beta pathway signaling, the conserved aortopathy mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Although Smad3-/- aortas showed increased nuclear pSmad2 and pErk, indicating TGF-β receptor activation, downstream TGF-β-activated target genes were not upregulated.
evidence.explanation: Refines the TGF-beta paradox: in the Smad3-null model, receptor-proximal signaling (pSmad2, pErk) is increased while downstream SMAD3-dependent target-gene transcription fails.

steps/3.description: Despite SMAD3 being a positive transducer of TGF-beta signaling, SMAD3 mutations lead to paradoxically increased expression of key TGF-beta pathway components in the aortic wall, the same dysregulated-TGF-beta signature seen across the heritable thoracic aortic disease syndromes.

evidence.snippet: However, early pathology was evident, with SMCs separated from elastic lamellae by a thin layer of glycosaminoglycans. Confocal reconstructions revealed that elastic fibers were poorly decorated by microfibrils, with reduced fibrillin-1, fibrillin-2, microfibril associated glycoprotein-2, fibulin-1 and fibulin-2.
evidence.explanation: Direct analysis of surgically obtained human aortas identifies an early tissue lesion preceding gross lamellar destruction.

steps/4.description: Early human aortic pathology in SMAD3 variant carriers consists of smooth muscle cells separated from elastic lamellae by glycosaminoglycans and elastic fibers that are poorly decorated by multiple microfibril proteins, even while lamellar structure and SMC content remain relatively intact.

evidence.snippet: We delineated a new syndrome presenting with aneurysms, dissections and tortuosity throughout the arterial tree
evidence.explanation: Establishes the systemic arterial-wall pathology (aneurysm, dissection, tortuosity) that reflects medial wall weakening.

evidence.snippet: Aortic wall immunohistochemistry showed no increase in extracellular matrix and collagen accumulation, nor loss of vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) but instead revealed medial elastin disruption and adventitial inflammation.
evidence.explanation: Identifies medial elastin disruption and adventitial inflammation (rather than SMC loss or ECM accumulation) as the medial-degeneration mechanism in the Smad3-null aorta.

evidence.snippet: the underlying mechanism involved aberrant upregulation of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-derived nitric oxide production and activation of elastolytic matrix metalloproteinases 2 and 9
evidence.explanation: Shows macrophage iNOS-derived nitric oxide and elastolytic MMP2/9 activation as the mechanism of wall weakening in SMAD3-deficient aortas.

steps/5.description: Dysregulated TGF-beta signaling together with the underlying connective tissue defect produces medial degeneration of the aortic wall. In the Smad3-null model the dominant findings are medial elastin (elastic fiber) disruption and adventitial inflammation with matrix metalloproteinase activation concentrated in inflammatory areas, progressively weakening the wall; this inflammatory, MMP-driven route is a notable AOS-specific feature.

evidence.snippet: In contrast with other aneurysm syndromes, most of these affected individuals presented with early-onset osteoarthritis
evidence.explanation: Establishes early-onset osteoarthritis as the distinctive musculoskeletal feature of the syndrome.

steps/6.description: A hallmark that distinguishes aneurysm-osteoarthritis syndrome from other aneurysm syndromes is prominent early-onset osteoarthritis, frequently with osteochondritis dissecans. SMAD3 is essential for TGF-beta-mediated regulation of chondrocyte differentiation and cartilage homeostasis, so its disruption promotes cartilage degeneration.

evidence.snippet: aneurysms, dissections and tortuosity throughout the arterial tree
evidence.explanation: Documents the widespread arterial aneurysm and tortuosity phenotype.

steps/7.description: Progressive weakening of the arterial wall produces aneurysms and marked tortuosity that, unlike Marfan syndrome, are distributed widely throughout the arterial tree rather than confined to the aortic root.

evidence.snippet: aortic dissection can occur at smaller aortic diameters and at younger ages than observed in Marfan syndrome; vascular disease is not limited to the aortic root
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents the high dissection risk at small diameters and the diffuse arterial involvement characteristic of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Of the patients who first presented with joint abnormalities, 20% died suddenly from aortic dissection.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the lethal risk of aortic dissection in AOS, including in patients who initially presented with joint disease.

evidence.snippet: Aortic events were documented in 37% of cases, with dissections accounting for 70% of events.
evidence.explanation: In an international SMAD3 cohort, aortic events (dissection or aneurysm repair) affected a substantial minority, most being dissections.

evidence.snippet: The main cause of death was aortic dissection (9 of 15; 60%), which occurred at mildly increased aortic diameters (range: 40 to 63 mm).
evidence.explanation: Aortic dissection was the leading cause of death and occurred at only mildly increased aortic diameters, underscoring dissection risk below conventional thresholds.

steps/8.description: The weakened, aneurysmal arterial wall is prone to dissection and rupture. A clinically critical feature shared with other Loeys-Dietz subtypes is that dissection can occur at smaller aortic diameters and at younger ages than in Marfan syndrome, and vascular disease is not limited to the aortic root.

evidence.snippet: Thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections are a main feature of connective tissue disorders
evidence.explanation: Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a defining vascular feature of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In 71%, an aortic root aneurysm was found.
evidence.explanation: In a cohort of 44 AOS patients, aortic root aneurysm was present in 71%, supporting a frequent occurrence.

steps/9.description: Aneurysm of the thoracic aorta, typically involving the aortic root, is a core vascular manifestation.

evidence.snippet: aortic dissection can occur at smaller aortic diameters and at younger ages than observed in Marfan syndrome
evidence.explanation: Documents aortic dissection and its occurrence at small diameters.

steps/10.description: Dissection of the aorta, which may occur at smaller diameters and younger ages than in Marfan syndrome.

evidence.snippet: aneurysms, dissections and tortuosity throughout the arterial tree
evidence.explanation: Arterial tortuosity throughout the arterial tree is a hallmark feature.

evidence.snippet: and in 48%, arterial tortuosity was diagnosed
evidence.explanation: Arterial tortuosity was diagnosed in 48% of the AOS cohort.

steps/11.description: Tortuosity of arteries throughout the arterial tree, a characteristic feature of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: vascular findings (cerebral, thoracic, and abdominal arterial aneurysms and/or dissections)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents cerebral arterial aneurysms as part of the LDS vascular spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Aneurysms and tortuosity were found in the aorta and other arteries throughout the body, including intracranial arteries.
evidence.explanation: AOS-specific cohort documents intracranial arterial aneurysms as part of the widespread arterial involvement.

evidence.snippet: cerebrovascular abnormalities were detected in 56% of
evidence.explanation: In AOS patients undergoing cerebrovascular imaging, abnormalities were detected in the majority (56%), supporting frequent cerebrovascular involvement.

steps/12.description: Intracranial arterial aneurysms occur as part of the widespread arterial involvement.

evidence.snippet: In 33%, aneurysms in other arteries in the thorax and abdomen were diagnosed
evidence.explanation: One third of the AOS cohort had aneurysms in arteries beyond the aortic root, in the thorax and abdomen.

evidence.snippet: The common iliac artery was most commonly affected (37%), followed by the superior mesenteric artery (15%), celiac trunk (11%), and splenic artery (9%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the distribution of visceral and iliac artery aneurysms in AOS, with the common iliac artery most affected.

steps/13.description: Aneurysms are widespread beyond the aorta, prominently involving the visceral (splanchnic) and iliac arteries. The common iliac artery is the most frequently affected branch, followed by superior mesenteric, celiac, and splenic arteries; early elective repair is recommended given very high rupture risk.

evidence.snippet: In contrast with other aneurysm syndromes, most of these affected individuals presented with early-onset osteoarthritis
evidence.explanation: Early-onset osteoarthritis is the distinguishing feature of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In the majority of patients, early-onset joint abnormalities, including osteoarthritis and osteochondritis dissecans, were the initial symptom for which medical advice was sought.
evidence.explanation: In the AOS phenotypic-spectrum cohort, early-onset osteoarthritis was the presenting feature in the majority of patients, supporting a very frequent occurrence.

steps/14.description: Premature, often generalized osteoarthritis with onset in childhood or early adulthood is the distinctive musculoskeletal hallmark of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In the majority of patients, early-onset joint abnormalities, including osteoarthritis and osteochondritis dissecans, were the initial symptom for which medical advice was sought.
evidence.explanation: Osteochondritis dissecans is explicitly reported among the early-onset joint abnormalities of AOS.

steps/15.description: Osteochondritis dissecans and other joint lesions accompany the early-onset osteoarthritis.

evidence.snippet: craniofacial features (hypertelorism, strabismus, bifid uvula / cleft palate, and craniosynostosis that can involve any sutures)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists hypertelorism among the craniofacial features of LDS.

steps/16.description: Increased distance between the eyes, a mild craniofacial feature.

evidence.snippet: bifid uvula / cleft palate
evidence.explanation: Bifid uvula/cleft palate is a recognized craniofacial feature.

steps/17.description: Bifid uvula or cleft palate, a craniofacial marker of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

evidence.snippet: skeletal manifestations (pectus excavatum or pectus carinatum, scoliosis, joint laxity, arachnodactyly, talipes equinovarus, and cervical spine malformation and/or instability)
evidence.explanation: Scoliosis is listed among the skeletal manifestations of LDS.

steps/18.description: Lateral curvature of the spine, part of the skeletal manifestations.

evidence.snippet: skeletal manifestations (pectus excavatum or pectus carinatum
evidence.explanation: Pectus deformity is a documented skeletal feature.

steps/19.description: Pectus excavatum or carinatum chest wall deformity.

evidence.snippet: Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS) is characterized by vascular findings (cerebral, thoracic, and abdominal arterial aneurysms and/or dissections), skeletal manifestations (pectus excavatum or pectus carinatum, scoliosis, joint laxity, arachnodactyly, talipes equinovarus, and cervical spine malformation and/or instability), craniofacial features (hypertelorism, strabismus, bifid uvula / cleft palate, and craniosynostosis that can involve any sutures), and cutaneous findings (velvety and translucent skin, easy bruising, and dystrophic scars).
evidence.explanation: Joint laxity is listed among the skeletal manifestations of LDS.

steps/20.description: Generalized joint hypermobility/laxity, which coexists with the degenerative joint disease.

evidence.snippet: cutaneous findings (velvety and translucent skin, easy bruising, and dystrophic scars)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents thin/translucent skin, easy bruising, and dystrophic scars among the cutaneous features of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

steps/21.description: Cutaneous fragility with velvety, thin/translucent skin, easy bruising, and dystrophic (atrophic) scars is part of the connective-tissue phenotype.

evidence.snippet: cardiac abnormalities were diagnosed, such as congenital heart defects (6%), mitral valve abnormalities (51%), left ventricular hypertrophy (19%), and atrial fibrillation (22%).
evidence.explanation: In the 44-patient AOS cohort, atrial fibrillation was present in 22%, which falls in the HPO OCCASIONAL band (5-29%).

steps/22.description: Atrial fibrillation is part of the cardiac phenotype of AOS, independent of the aortic disease.

evidence.snippet: cardiac abnormalities were diagnosed, such as congenital heart defects (6%), mitral valve abnormalities (51%), left ventricular hypertrophy (19%), and atrial fibrillation (22%).
evidence.explanation: In the 44-patient AOS cohort, left ventricular hypertrophy was present in 19%, which falls in the HPO OCCASIONAL band (5-29%).

steps/23.description: Left ventricular hypertrophy is observed as part of the broader cardiac involvement in AOS.

evidence.snippet: LDS Type 3 demonstrated an increased prevalence of mitral valve prolapse and arthritis
evidence.explanation: A systematic review reports increased mitral valve prolapse (and arthritis) specifically in SMAD3-related LDS type 3.

evidence.snippet: mitral valve abnormalities (51%)
evidence.explanation: Mitral valve abnormalities were present in 51% of the AOS cohort.

evidence.snippet: There was significant intrafamilial phenotypic variability within the cohort with the predominant cardiovascular abnormality being mitral valve disease followed by aortic disease.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in SMAD3, encoding the receptor-regulated SMAD3 of the TGF-beta pathway, cause aneurysm-osteoarthritis syndrome (Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 3). Inheritance is autosomal dominant. The variant spectrum includes haploinsufficiency alleles and missense substitutions in the MH2 domain (as well as MH1-domain variants and in-frame deletions); MH2 missense variants are associated with earlier aortic events. Penetrance for aortic disease is reduced and age of onset is variable.

open_questions/0.rationale: The entry models an ARB -> "TGF-beta Signaling Dysregulation" INHIBITS edge, but that edge is not directly evidenced in AOS. The GeneReviews statement attached to the ARB treatment supports only reduction of hemodynamic stress, not TGF-beta inhibition. Two SMAD3 mouse studies point away from TGF-beta as the actionable target: PMID:27688095 concludes that immune suppression may be more beneficial than targeting TGF-beta signaling, and PMID:23782924 nominates macrophage depletion and iNOS antagonism instead. The paradoxical-TGF-beta-increase model is inherited from the aortopathy_tgfbeta_dysregulation module and from Marfan/losartan biology, so there is a real risk of importing a mechanism that has not been demonstrated for SMAD3 specifically. Resolving this matters clinically, since ARB therapy is a modeled treatment for this disease.

Discuss recessive inheritance, variable severity and reproductive options using variant-specific interpretation. Mild biochemical changes in some heterozygotes do not convert the established recessive disorder into a uniformly dominant disease.

evidence.snippet: Nonclassic AME (NC-AME) is mainly related to partial 11βHSD2 deficiency associated with genetic variations and epigenetic modifications (first hit) and potential additive actions of endogenous or exogenous inhibitors (ie, glycyrrhetinic acid-like factors [GALFS]) and other factors (ie, age, high sodium intake) (second hit).

evidence.snippet: Despite that there is no prospective data in NC-AME, inference from PA studies support the concept of improved renin levels as a proxy of MR inactivation

open_questions/2.rationale: The 2020 review describes a broader partial-enzyme-deficiency construct involving genetic, epigenetic, environmental and inhibitor effects. This should not automatically be equated with genetically confirmed mild recessive AME. Its 7.1% estimate comes from a particular screening population and is not the prevalence of biallelic HSD11B2 disease. The screening construct used high serum cortisol/cortisone together with low cortisone in a selected Chilean population including normotensive and hypertensive people. Renin-guided outcome benefit is extrapolated from primary aldosteronism, not demonstrated prospectively in nonclassic AME.

evidence.snippet: These results indicate that SYNGAP1 disruption is a cause of autosomal dominant nonsyndromic mental retardation.

evidence.snippet: In two individuals, variants were inherited from a similarly affected parent, while all other variants (n = 34) occurred de novo.
evidence.explanation: The TLK2 series includes inherited and de novo variants; two additional probands had unknown inheritance. One affected mother had low-normal IQ, so dominant inheritance does not imply complete penetrance for ID.

evidence.snippet: We estimate that 42% of our cohort carry pathogenic DNMs in coding sequences; approximately half of these DNMs disrupt gene function and the remainder result in altered protein function.
evidence.explanation: The broader DDD cohort supports multiple mechanisms. Its modeled proportions are not AD-NSID penetrance or diagnostic yield.

steps/10.description: Heterozygous coding variants, splice variants or structural disruptions can arise de novo or be inherited. A pathogenic effect requires gene- and allele-specific evidence; rarity, de novo occurrence and population constraint alone do not establish causality. Loss of function and altered activity lead to different downstream branches. Candidate regulatory variants are discussed separately as an emerging hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: By analyzing TLK2 transcripts in cell lines of three different individuals, we were able to confirm that transcripts were subjected to NMD in two of them, causing haploinsufficiency of TLK2.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived fibroblast and lymphoblastoid experiments support nonsense-mediated decay for two tested alleles; the tested last-exon stop variant escaped decay.

evidence.snippet: both the protein and RNA levels of CIC were reduced to almost 50%
evidence.explanation: Measured in fibroblasts from one CIC patient; this is direct dosage evidence for that allele, not a universal 50% rule.

steps/11.description: Reduced functional dosage is an established mechanism for particular genes and variants. Transcript decay or loss of protein function can leave insufficient activity for neuronal development and function. The magnitude of reduction is assay- and allele-dependent, and a population constraint score is not a direct protein-dosage measurement. This branch does not represent activating or other altered-function alleles.

evidence.snippet: although CAMK2GArg292Pro has reduced protein stability, this mutation does not lead to a loss of function of CAMK2G, but instead appears to result in a paradoxical gain‐of‐function.
evidence.explanation: HEK293T and primary-neuron expression experiments distinguish increased activity from reduced abundance. The developmental migration assay was separately performed in mouse embryos.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, both loss-of-function and gain-of-function KCNQ5 mutations, associated with increased excitability and decreased repolarization reserve, lead to pathophysiology.
evidence.explanation: Frog-oocyte electrophysiology establishes altered channel function for tested KCNQ5 alleles. The proposed consequences for patient neurons remain an inference.

steps/12.description: Activating and other altered-function alleles require functional interpretation separate from protein abundance. CAMK2G p.Arg292Pro increases kinase activity despite reduced protein stability; KCNQ5 variants can increase or decrease channel function. These findings do not establish one direction of neuronal excitability for all affected genes. AP2M1 p.Arg170Trp impairs adaptor-complex function without decreasing expression or stability in the tested cell systems.

evidence.snippet: Systematic identification of highly enriched functional themes and phenotypes revealed typical phenotype combinations characterizing process-defined groups of ID disorders, such as chromatin-related disorders and deficiencies in DNA repair.
evidence.explanation: Establishes chromatin regulation as a distinct, statistically coherent functional module among ID-associated genes.

evidence.snippet: we show that ID-AGs are substantially enriched with co-expression, protein-protein interactions, and specific biological functions.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that the genetically heterogeneous ID gene set is functionally convergent rather than random.

evidence.snippet: A total of 12 likely pathogenic DNMs were identified in genes previously associated with ID (ARID1B, CHD2, FOXG1, GABRB3, GATAD2B, GRIN2B, MBD5, MED13L, SETBP1, TBR1, TCF4, WDR45), resulting in a diagnostic yield of ∼29%.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal dominant non-syndromic intellectual disability 22 is a rare genetic disorder caused by the ZBTB18 gene.
evidence.explanation: A ZBTB18-associated clinical diagnosis; the case report alone does not measure protein dosage or establish the mechanism of every allele.

evidence.snippet: Emerging evidence highlights the critical status of these chromatin remodeling molecules in dendritic spine morphogenesis and synaptic functions.
evidence.explanation: Links the chromatin module to the same dendritic-spine and synaptic endpoint as the synaptic module, supporting the convergence of the two arms rather than treating them as parallel unrelated pathways.

steps/13.description: Chromatin modifiers and transcriptional regulators affect developmental gene expression through diverse mechanisms. Dosage loss is demonstrated for selected alleles, while missense variants can have distinct effects. Computational clustering identifies chromatin-related groups among broader ID-associated genes; it does not prove that every gene reduces protein abundance by half or changes the same targets.

evidence.snippet: Functional complementation of both the μ-subunit carrying the p.Arg170Trp variant in human cells and astrocytes derived from AP-2μ conditional knockout mice revealed a significant impairment of CME of transferrin.

steps/14.description: AP2M1 p.Arg170Trp impairs AP-2-dependent endocytosis without reduced expression, stability or membrane recruitment in the tested systems. This is a variant-specific trafficking mechanism distinct from haploinsufficiency. Its contribution to neuronal synaptic function is inferred from AP-2 biology rather than directly measured by the transferrin assay.

evidence.snippet: Mutations that cause intellectual disability (ID) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are commonly found in genes that encode for synaptic proteins.
evidence.explanation: States the synaptic-gene convergence that defines this pathophysiology module.

evidence.snippet: We sequenced the autosomal gene SYNGAP1, which encodes a ras GTPase-activating protein that is critical for cognition and synapse function, in 94 patients with nonsyndromic mental retardation.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the molecular function (Ras GTPase-activating protein) whose loss underlies the paradigmatic AD-NSID gene.

evidence.snippet: SYNGAP1, a GTPase-activating protein that is selectively expressed in the brain and is a component of the NMDA-receptor complex, acts downstream of the receptor, blocking the insertion of the AMPA receptor at the postsynaptic membrane
evidence.explanation: Describes the specific postsynaptic signalling step (restraint of AMPA receptor insertion via inhibition of RAS-ERK) that haploinsufficiency de-represses.

evidence.snippet: We sequenced genes coding for components of the SNARE complex (STX1A, VAMP2, SNAP25) and their regulatory proteins (STXBP1/Munc18-1, SYT1), which are essential for neurotransmission, in 95 patients with idiopathic mental retardation.
evidence.explanation: Extends the synaptic module to the presynaptic release machinery, identifying STXBP1 as an AD-NSID gene.

evidence.snippet: The classic observation that various forms of mental retardation are associated with abnormalities in the morphology of dendritic spines suggests that disruption of pathways involved in synaptic plasticity may be a common mechanism of this disorder.
evidence.explanation: States the long-standing convergence of ID pathophysiology on dendritic spine morphology and synaptic plasticity.

steps/15.description: Representative synaptic genes affect postsynaptic signaling, receptor trafficking or presynaptic vesicle release. SYNGAP1 restrains Ras-associated signaling and AMPA receptor insertion; STXBP1 participates in presynaptic release. Other genes and alleles have distinct effects. These routes can disturb plasticity without implying that every subtype has increased excitatory transmission.

evidence.snippet: Bibliomic analysis reveals that ID genes converge onto a few biological modules, including cytoskeleton dynamics, whose regulation depends on Rho GTPases transduction.
evidence.explanation: Establishes cytoskeletal dynamics under Rho GTPase control as one of the small number of convergent biological modules among ID genes.

evidence.snippet: Thus, cytoskeleton alterations that have an impact on cell processes such as neuronal migration, neuritogenesis, and synaptic plasticity rebound on the overall establishment of an effective network and consequently on the cognitive phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Specifies the cellular processes disrupted and the propagation from cytoskeletal lesion through network formation to cognition.

evidence.snippet: More than 1000 genes have been found mutated in ID patients pointing out that, despite the common phenotype, the genetic bases are highly heterogeneous and apparently unrelated.

evidence.snippet: The p.N1080I mutant (in individual 6) did not affect Trio-mediated Rac1 activation.
evidence.explanation: HEK293T pull-down assays found reduced Rac1 activation for three other tested variants, demonstrating that the result is allele-specific.

steps/16.description: Cytoskeletal regulators influence neuronal migration, neurite growth and later synaptic function. In TRIO, selected GEF1-domain variants reduce Rac1 activation, whereas another tested variant outside that domain did not alter that assay. Cytoskeletal and synaptic processes overlap in time; this module is not necessarily upstream of all synaptic defects.

evidence.snippet: In the SYNGAP1 mouse model of ID/ASD, we found that dendritic spine synapses develop prematurely during the early postnatal period.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates accelerated dendritic spine synapse maturation in a genetic mouse model of AD-NSID.

steps/17.description: In the cited SYNGAP1 mouse model, reduced SynGAP dosage accelerates early postnatal dendritic spine-synapse maturation. This establishes a developmental phenotype in that model; it does not show that timing is the sole determinant of later function or that adult restoration cannot improve selected outcomes.

evidence.snippet: These data demonstrate that SynGAP protein acts as a critical developmental repressor of neural excitability that promotes the development of life-long cognitive abilities.
evidence.explanation: Frames the gene product's normal role as a developmental brake on excitability whose loss produces the hyperexcitable state.

steps/18.description: SYNGAP1 mouse studies demonstrate increased excitability in developing hippocampal circuits. Later experiments also implicate ongoing adult SynGAP function in seizure susceptibility and interictal discharges. These findings are not a universal excitation model for every dominant ID subtype.

evidence.snippet: Inducing SYNGAP1 mutations after critical developmental windows closed had minimal impact on spine synapse function, whereas repairing these pathogenic mutations in adulthood did not improve behavior and cognition.
evidence.explanation: The earlier mouse experiment reported failure to rescue the tested behaviors in adulthood. Later experiments used different endpoints and found substantial adult reversibility.

evidence.snippet: We propose that the pace of dendritic spine synapse maturation in early life is a critical determinant of normal intellectual development.
evidence.explanation: States the developmental-timing model linking synaptic maturation pace to intellectual outcome.

evidence.snippet: genetic reversal ofSyngap1pathogenicity in adult mice reverses deficits in remote memory
evidence.explanation: Adult genetic restoration improved remote contextual memory in mice; this is endpoint-specific preclinical evidence and does not establish human therapeutic efficacy.

steps/19.description: Changes in neuronal maturation and connectivity can contribute to cognitive impairment, while ongoing gene function also remains relevant in mature circuits. Earlier SYNGAP1 mouse experiments found developmental restrictions for particular behavioral outcomes. Later adult restoration rescued remote contextual memory and selected seizure and electrophysiological outcomes, while some other behaviors remained abnormal. These model-specific results do not establish a universal early deadline for human treatment.

evidence.snippet: The absence of specific dysmorphic features and growth abnormalities in these patients is consistent with the fact that SYNGAP1 is exclusively expressed in the brain.
evidence.explanation: An interpretation of three selected SYNGAP1 cases in the 2009 paper; brain expression does not prove that all associated clinical findings are restricted to cognition.

evidence.snippet: Most patients have the nonsyndromic form of the disorder, which is characterized by the absence of associated morphologic, radiologic, and metabolic features.
evidence.explanation: Defines the non-syndromic category operationally.

evidence.snippet: patients with DNMs in the same novel DD-associated gene were less phenotypically similar to each other, on average, than patients with DNMs in a consensus gene
evidence.explanation: Phenotypic-similarity analysis in a broader developmental-disorder cohort; it supports an ascertainment hypothesis rather than proving every newly discovered gene is non-syndromic.

steps/20.description: Intellectual and adaptive impairment begins during development. Severity and trajectory vary by diagnosis; a lack of a recognizable syndrome at presentation does not prove brain-restricted biology, absence of other features or a uniformly static course. Some gene-associated cohorts include regression or individuals without formal intellectual disability.

evidence.snippet: We then sequenced the coding regions of more than 21,000 genes obtained from 100 patients with an IQ below 50 and their unaffected parents.

evidence.snippet: Scores on the Mullen Scales of Early Learning and the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales showed profiles that were consistent with moderate-to-severe mental retardation in all patients.

steps/21.description: Significantly impaired intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour with onset in the developmental period. Severity across the AD-NSID class spans mild to severe; cohorts ascertained for trio exome sequencing have been enriched for moderate-to-severe disability (e.g. IQ below 50).

evidence.snippet: Two of the patients were mildly epileptic.

evidence.snippet: We identified de novo mutations in STXBP1 (nonsense, p.R388X; splicing, c.169+1G>A) in two patients with severe mental retardation and nonsyndromic epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: However, he did not have growth retardation, microcephaly, corpus callosum hypoplasia, epilepsy, or dysmorphic facial features.

steps/22.description: Epilepsy is a common comorbidity in several AD-NSID entities, ranging from well-controlled generalised seizures to a pharmacoresistant developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Its presence is one of the features that most often triggers reclassification of a nominally non-syndromic gene-disease pair as a recognisable syndrome; conversely, some MRD-series entities (e.g. ZBTB18/MRD22) present without epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: By analyzing TLK2 transcripts in cell lines of three different individuals, we were able to confirm that transcripts were subjected to NMD in two of them, causing haploinsufficiency of TLK2.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived fibroblast and lymphoblastoid experiments support nonsense-mediated decay for two tested alleles; the tested last-exon stop variant escaped decay.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, both loss-of-function and gain-of-function KCNQ5 mutations, associated with increased excitability and decreased repolarization reserve, lead to pathophysiology.
evidence.explanation: Frog-oocyte electrophysiology establishes altered channel function for tested KCNQ5 alleles. The proposed consequences for patient neurons remain an inference.

evidence.snippet: In the SYNGAP1 mouse model of ID/ASD, we found that dendritic spine synapses develop prematurely during the early postnatal period. Premature spine maturation dramatically enhanced excitability in the developing hippocampus, which corresponded with the emergence of behavioral abnormalities.

edges/20.description: In the SYNGAP1 model, de-repressed excitatory synaptic signalling accelerates spine maturation and raises circuit excitability.

edges/21.description: Dysregulated transcriptional programmes alter neuronal differentiation and connectivity during cortical development.

evidence.snippet: Emerging evidence highlights the critical status of these chromatin remodeling molecules in dendritic spine morphogenesis and synaptic functions.

evidence.snippet: Thus, cytoskeleton alterations that have an impact on cell processes such as neuronal migration, neuritogenesis, and synaptic plasticity rebound on the overall establishment of an effective network and consequently on the cognitive phenotype.
evidence.explanation: A review-level mechanistic synthesis, not direct experimental proof of every intervening step.

edges/23.description: Disrupted migration, neurite development and plasticity can alter circuit organization through gene-specific intermediates.

evidence.snippet: Premature spine maturation dramatically enhanced excitability in the developing hippocampus, which corresponded with the emergence of behavioral abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from mistimed spine maturation to hyperexcitability in the same model.

edges/24.description: Prematurely mature spines drive excessive excitability in the developing hippocampus.

evidence.snippet: We propose that the pace of dendritic spine synapse maturation in early life is a critical determinant of normal intellectual development.
evidence.explanation: An explicit mechanistic proposal rather than a demonstration that hyperexcitability alone causes cognitive impairment.

evidence.snippet: Adult restoration of SynGAP protein improved behavioral and electrophysiological measures of memory and seizure.
evidence.explanation: Adult mouse genetic restoration supports an ongoing contribution to seizure-related physiology; it is indirect evidence for the human causal path.

edges/26.description: In SYNGAP1-related disease, altered excitability contributes to seizure susceptibility. Human epilepsy observations and adult mouse restoration support this route without establishing the intermediates or its applicability to every subtype.

evidence.snippet: Thus, cytoskeleton alterations that have an impact on cell processes such as neuronal migration, neuritogenesis, and synaptic plasticity rebound on the overall establishment of an effective network and consequently on the cognitive phenotype.
evidence.explanation: A review-level mechanistic synthesis, not direct experimental proof of every intervening step.

edges/27.description: Altered neural development and ongoing circuit function can contribute to cognitive and adaptive impairment through subtype-specific intermediates.

evidence.snippet: These results indicate that SYNGAP1 disruption is a cause of autosomal dominant nonsyndromic mental retardation.
evidence.explanation: The SYNGAP1 cases provide a clinical example of the intellectual-disability endpoint; this edge names the manifestation of intellectual and adaptive impairment rather than a separate molecular step.

edges/28.description: The clinical phenotype records the intellectual and adaptive impairment represented by this terminal disease process.

evidence.snippet: We identified de novo truncating mutations (K138X, R579X, and L813RfsX22) in three of these patients.
evidence.explanation: Three independent de novo protein-truncating variants in 94 patients with non-syndromic ID.

evidence.snippet: We provide evidence that truncating mutations in SYNGAP1 are common in NSID and can be also associated with autism.
evidence.explanation: The replication study identified three variants in 60 additional selected sporadic cases, including one patient with autism. Its reference to three of 94 in the background describes the original cohort.

genes/0.notes: MRD5. The paradigmatic AD-NSID gene: a brain-restricted Ras GTPase-activating protein in the NMDA receptor complex. Note that larger later series redescribe SYNGAP1 disease as a recognisable developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, making it the clearest worked example of the non-syndromic-to-syndromic migration.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that STXBP1 disruption is associated with autosomal dominant mental retardation and nonsyndromic epilepsy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes STXBP1 as an autosomal dominant non-syndromic ID gene.

evidence.snippet: 16 patients carried de-novo variants in known intellectual disability genes with three recurrently mutated genes (STXBP1, SYNGAP1, and SCN2A).
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of STXBP1 recurrence in a severe sporadic non-syndromic ID cohort.

genes/1.notes: Encodes Munc18-1, an essential regulator of SNARE-mediated synaptic vesicle fusion. One of the three recurrently mutated genes in the Rauch severe sporadic non-syndromic ID cohort.

evidence.snippet: Clinical whole exome sequencing revealed a de novo pathogenic variant in the ZBTB18 gene (c.1207delC, p. Arg403Alafs*60), which is a previously unreported site.
evidence.explanation: De novo frameshift variant in a patient diagnosed with MRD22.

evidence.snippet: It is noteworthy that only 31 cases of this disorder have been reported thus far.
evidence.explanation: A historical count reported in the 2024 article, not a current census or causal explanation of diagnostic classification.

genes/2.notes: MRD22. ZBTB18 encodes a transcriptional repressor. The 2024 case report counted 31 previously reported cases; that historical count is neither current prevalence nor proof that the phenotype remains non-syndromic.

evidence.snippet: A total of 12 likely pathogenic DNMs were identified in genes previously associated with ID (ARID1B, CHD2, FOXG1, GABRB3, GATAD2B, GRIN2B, MBD5, MED13L, SETBP1, TBR1, TCF4, WDR45), resulting in a diagnostic yield of ∼29%.
evidence.explanation: GRIN2B recovered as a de novo cause in a moderate-to-severe ID trio cohort.

genes/3.notes: MRD6. Encodes the GluN2B subunit of the NMDA receptor - the receptor complex that SYNGAP1 also acts within - placing it squarely in the synaptic module.

evidence.snippet: A total of 12 likely pathogenic DNMs were identified in genes previously associated with ID (ARID1B, CHD2, FOXG1, GABRB3, GATAD2B, GRIN2B, MBD5, MED13L, SETBP1, TBR1, TCF4, WDR45), resulting in a diagnostic yield of ∼29%.
evidence.explanation: GATAD2B recovered as a de novo cause in a moderate-to-severe ID trio cohort.

genes/4.notes: A subunit of the NuRD chromatin-remodelling complex; a member of the chromatin/transcription module.

evidence.snippet: A total of 12 likely pathogenic DNMs were identified in genes previously associated with ID (ARID1B, CHD2, FOXG1, GABRB3, GATAD2B, GRIN2B, MBD5, MED13L, SETBP1, TBR1, TCF4, WDR45), resulting in a diagnostic yield of ∼29%.
evidence.explanation: Supports MED13L as a dominant ID gene in a cohort selected by severity, not by absence of syndromic features.

genes/5.notes: MED13L encodes a Mediator-complex subunit. It is retained as a historical dominant-ID example; the cited severity-selected cohort does not establish membership in a non-syndromic category. Gene-specific clinical interpretation belongs to MED13L syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Trio is a Dbl family guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) and a major regulator of neuronal development, controlling actin cytoskeleton dynamics by activating the GTPase Rac1.
evidence.explanation: Places TRIO in the cytoskeletal/Rho GTPase pathophysiology module.

evidence.snippet: We identified a frameshift deletion in TRIO that segregated autosomal dominantly. By scrutinising data from DDD, we further identified three unrelated children with a similar phenotype who harboured de novo missense mutations in TRIO.
evidence.explanation: Documents both an inherited autosomal dominant lesion and de novo lesions in the same gene, supporting the caveat that AD-NSID is not exclusively a de novo class.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, we identify pathogenic de novo missense mutations in TRIO associated with the same consistent phenotype, intellectual disability, microcephaly and dysmorphism with striking digital features.
evidence.explanation: The reported microcephaly and dysmorphism limit the use of this series as evidence for a non-syndromic category.

genes/6.notes: Illustrates the cytoskeletal/Rho GTPase module: TRIO is a Dbl-family guanine nucleotide exchange factor that activates Rac1 and controls actin dynamics in developing neurons. Included here with two explicit caveats that make it instructive rather than clean. First, the best-characterised TRIO series reports microcephaly and dysmorphism alongside the ID, so this gene-disease pair sits on the syndromic side of an unstable boundary. Second, that series includes an autosomal dominant frameshift that SEGREGATED through a family as well as de novo missense variants, demonstrating that the class is not exclusively de novo. Both caveats argue against treating "autosomal dominant" and "de novo" as synonyms. A third caveat is that the head-size feature is not directionally fixed: TRIO-related disease includes both MRD44 with microcephaly and MRD63 with macrocephaly. The dedicated TRIO-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder entry now models that domain-resolved, RAC1-direction-dependent split and is the canonical home for TRIO variants and mechanisms. TRIO is retained here only as a boundary exemplar, not as a clean non-syndromic gene; the cephalic and dysmorphic findings illustrate why umbrella AD-NSID membership is partial (see GitHub issue 6041).

evidence.snippet: Through a multi-center collaborative study based on a whole-exome sequencing approach, we identified 19 exceedingly rare de novo CAMK2A or CAMK2B variants in 24 unrelated individuals with intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Establishes CAMK2A as a de novo heterozygous cause of intellectual disability in a multi-centre trio-sequencing cohort.

evidence.snippet: We further found that all mutations affecting auto-phosphorylation also affected neuronal migration, highlighting the importance of tightly regulated CAMK2 auto-phosphorylation in neuronal function and neurodevelopment.
evidence.explanation: Neuronal migration was tested after in-utero electroporation of E14.5 mouse embryos; cultured-cell phosphorylation assays were separate. This is preclinical mechanism evidence, not a direct patient measurement.

genes/7.notes: Included because Open Targets lists CAMK2A among the genes associated with MONDO:0015802 specifically, anchoring this entry to the curated umbrella entity rather than to the general de novo ID literature. The alpha subunit of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II - a synaptic-module gene whose autophosphorylation state governs plasticity and neuronal migration.

evidence.snippet: The clinical picture was predominated by early onset global developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder, all of which point to a brain disorder.
evidence.explanation: Predominantly neurodevelopmental findings in the 53-person series; this does not demonstrate absence of extra-neurological manifestations.

evidence.snippet: despite some overlapping features, a distinct facial dysmorphism could not be established
evidence.explanation: Explicit negative finding for a recognisable dysmorphic gestalt, supporting non-syndromic classification on positive grounds rather than by default.

genes/8.notes: DLG4 encodes the postsynaptic scaffold PSD-95. The cited 53-person series found prominent neurodevelopmental features without a distinct facial gestalt; this does not establish exclusively cerebral biology. The dedicated DLG4-related synaptopathy entry carries gene-specific clinical detail.

evidence.snippet: Recently, deleterious heterozygous variants in KMT5B were implicated in individuals with intellectual disability (ID) and/or autism spectrum disorder.
evidence.explanation: Establishes heterozygous KMT5B variants as a cause of intellectual disability, placing the gene in the chromatin/transcription module.

evidence.snippet: suggest that this gene should be considered in the differential diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders accompanied by macrocephaly and/or overgrowth
evidence.explanation: Recurrent macrocephaly or overgrowth suggests a broader clinical pattern and limits a strictly non-syndromic interpretation; one feature alone is not a syndromic diagnosis.

genes/9.notes: A histone H4K20 methyltransferase; a chromatin/transcription-module gene listed by Open Targets against MONDO:0015802. Included with the caveat that the associated macrocephaly/overgrowth is itself a recognisable feature, so KMT5B is a further candidate for migration out of the non-syndromic class.

evidence.snippet: DPP6 | HGNC:3010 | complex neurodevelopmental disorder | MONDO:0100038 | AD | Disputed | SOP8 | Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel
evidence.explanation: The expert-panel classification itself: Disputed, not Definitive or Limited.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, the available genetic evidence fails to support a role for heterozygous disruption of DPP6 in ID, autism or other neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence.explanation: The panel's summary judgement, which is the reason MONDO:0014580 has no subtype row on this entry.

evidence.snippet: Given the lack of evidence supporting their role in disease and the fact that no other DPP6 variants have been reported in association with microcephaly and ID, these variants were not scored.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the panel examined the same variants the MRD33 concept is built on and declined to score them, so this is a re-assessment of the founding evidence rather than an independent negative study.

evidence.snippet: Our data indicate that the loss-of-function variations in DPP6 are associated with autosomal dominant microcephaly and mental retardation.
evidence.explanation: The original report the MRD33 concept rests on, recorded so the disputed claim is visible alongside the dispute rather than only asserted against. Note that even as stated it describes microcephaly, not isolated non-syndromic intellectual disability.

genes/10.notes: Recorded as a disposition, not as a cause. MONDO asserts `intellectual disability, autosomal dominant 33` (MONDO:0014580) as a direct subclass of this entry's own term and defines it as any autosomal dominant non-syndromic intellectual disability caused by a mutation in DPP6. No `has_subtypes` row was created for MONDO:0014580, because ClinGen's Intellectual Disability and Autism Gene Curation Expert Panel classifies the DPP6 gene-disease relationship as Disputed and states that no valid evidence remains to support it. The panel re-examined the same 2013 microcephaly variants that the OMIM and MONDO concept rests on and did not score them. DPP6 is curated elsewhere in this knowledge base for an unrelated cardiac phenotype (`Paroxysmal_Familial_Ventricular_Fibrillation`); nothing here bears on that.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that somatic mosaicism for transmitted mutations among parents of children with simplex genetic disease is more common than currently appreciated.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that apparently de novo variants in simplex cases can arise from underdetected parental mosaicism, the basis for a non-zero recurrence-risk counselling message.

evidence.snippet: Integrated probabilistic modeling of gametogenesis developed in response to our observations predicts that mutations in parental blood increase recurrence risk substantially more than parental mutations confined to the germline.
evidence.explanation: A probabilistic model of genomic-disorder recurrence, not an individualized risk rule inferred from blood mosaicism.

evidence.snippet: Here we present 12 cases of apparent mosaicism identified in the CAUSES cohort: nine cases of parental mosaicism for a disease-causing variant found in a child and three cases of mosaicism in the proband for a de novo variant.
evidence.explanation: Mosaicism found in 500 trios referred for suspected genetic disease, not an unselected population or an AD-NSID-specific frequency.

evidence.snippet: In six of these cases, there was no evidence of mosaicism on Sanger sequencing-the variant was not detected on Sanger sequencing in three cases, and it appeared to be heterozygous in three others.
evidence.explanation: Sanger sequencing did not identify mosaicism in six of these twelve selected cases. This is not an estimate of test sensitivity for all mosaic variants.

treatments/0.description: Genetic counseling uses the molecular result, parental testing and phenotype to assess recurrence. Apparently de novo variants can reflect parental somatic or germline mosaicism. A negative blood test does not exclude germline mosaicism, and the blood variant fraction is not an individual gamete-based recurrence probability. The broader genomic-disorder models cited here do not provide one recurrence rate for all AD-NSID.

evidence.snippet: INTERVENTIONS: Rehabilitation training.
evidence.explanation: Rehabilitation was reported in one ZBTB18 case; treatment use alone does not demonstrate efficacy or absence of other therapeutic options.

evidence.snippet: Educational support is a crucial component of the management of intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: General intellectual-disability care guidance supports educational services tailored to individual needs; it is not evidence of molecular correction or an AD-NSID-specific treatment effect.

treatments/1.description: Management includes individualized developmental, educational and rehabilitation support. Needs and services vary by age, function and molecular diagnosis. The cited evidence does not establish a universal treatment deadline or a single disease-modifying treatment status across all gene-associated disorders.

evidence.snippet: The disruption of SYNGAP1 appears to be associated with a homogeneous clinical phenotype that is characterized by moderate-to-severe mental retardation accompanied by severe language impairment.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the language impairment that this therapy targets; the citation supports the indication, not the efficacy of the intervention.

treatments/2.description: Communication support is tailored to language and adaptive needs. Severe language impairment in SYNGAP1 motivates assessment and intervention, but the discovery series does not evaluate speech-therapy efficacy.

evidence.snippet: Hypotonia and unstable gait were frequent associated neurological features.
evidence.explanation: Documents the motor impairments that motivate physiotherapy; supports the indication rather than the efficacy.

treatments/3.description: Motor and adaptive support is tailored to hypotonia, delayed walking and gait difficulties when present. The cited SYNGAP1 phenotype series identifies treatment needs but does not establish the efficacy of physical or occupational therapy.

evidence.snippet: Indeed, topiramate directly inhibits AMPA-receptor activity, whereas valproate reduces the level of GluR1 AMPA-receptor subunit at hippocampal synapses and therefore indirectly reduces AMPA-receptor activity.
evidence.explanation: Gives the mechanistic rationale linking drug choice to the AMPA-receptor-mediated hyperexcitability node; this is authors' interpretation, not a controlled comparison.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were pharmacoresistant in half of the patients.
evidence.explanation: The larger series reports pharmacoresistance in half of patients. The remaining patients cannot automatically be counted as seizure-free, and this is not a category-wide response rate.

treatments/4.description: When epilepsy is present, standard antiseizure medication is used. Response is variable and gene-dependent: seizures were well controlled by topiramate or valproate in the original SYNGAP1 series, whereas roughly half the patients in a larger SYNGAP1 cohort were pharmacoresistant. There is a mechanistic rationale for AMPA-directed agents in SYNGAP1 haploinsufficiency, but it is a hypothesis generated from mouse work and small case observations, not a validated precision-therapy indication.

evidence.snippet: Indeed, topiramate directly inhibits AMPA-receptor activity, whereas valproate reduces the level of GluR1 AMPA-receptor subunit at hippocampal synapses and therefore indirectly reduces AMPA-receptor activity.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic rationale for the drug acting on the hyperexcitability node; authors' interpretation rather than a controlled trial.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: The authors proposed reduced AMPA-associated excitation as one rationale for observed seizure responses. This is not a complete account of either drug's action and does not establish precision efficacy or absence of cognitive benefit.

evidence.snippet: Patient 1 had brief, generalized tonic–clonic seizures and was seizure-free while taking topiramate
evidence.explanation: Seizure freedom in one reported SYNGAP1 patient; an uncontrolled observation, not comparative efficacy.

treatments/5.description: Seizure freedom in one reported SYNGAP1 patient; an uncontrolled observation, not comparative efficacy.

evidence.snippet: Patient 2 had some myoclonic and absence seizures, which were well controlled with valproate.
evidence.explanation: Reported seizure control in a second SYNGAP1 patient; an uncontrolled observation, not a precision-treatment indication.

treatments/6.description: Reported seizure control in a second SYNGAP1 patient; an uncontrolled observation, not a precision-treatment indication.

evidence.snippet: Several patients did not meet the expected syndromic manifestation, suggesting a strong bias in present clinical syndrome descriptions.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly attributes syndromic/non-syndromic misclassification to bias in existing clinical syndrome descriptions.

evidence.snippet: The large number of de-novo variants in known intellectual disability genes is only partially attributable to known non-specific phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Notes that patients ascertained as non-syndromic frequently carry variants in genes catalogued as syndromic.

evidence.snippet: SYNGAP1 encephalopathy is characterised by early neurodevelopmental delay typically preceding the onset of a relatively recognisable epilepsy comprising generalised seizures (absences, myoclonic jerks) and frequent triggers.
evidence.explanation: Worked example of the predicted migration: SYNGAP1, first reported as a cause of NON-syndromic ID, is redescribed as a recognisable developmental and epileptic encephalopathy once a larger series is phenotyped.

hypotheses/0.description: The non-syndromic label can reflect the phenotype recognized at a particular age and depth of assessment. Larger gene-specific series may reveal recurrent clinical patterns. Tissue expression may influence presentation but does not by itself prove an exclusively cognitive phenotype. These explanations can coexist; this category does not establish a unique common disease mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We found that regulatory DNMs were selectively enriched in fetal brain-specific enhancers as compared with adult brain enhancers.
evidence.explanation: Enrichment among regulatory candidates in a small, selected severe-ID cohort; it does not establish every variant as disease-causing.

evidence.snippet: Using CRISPR-mediated mutation and editing of epigenomic marks, we show that DNMs at regulatory elements affect the expression of putative target genes.
