evidence.snippet: In the present study, we report a novel homozygous missense (NM_015239: c.2447A > C, p. Gln816Pro) variant in the AGTPBP1 gene that c.2447A > C variant has never been reported in a homozygous state in the Genome Aggregation (gnomAD; v2.1.1) database, identified by whole-exome sequencing in a patient with a seizure, dystonia, dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), and accompanying atrophy of caudate nuclei, putamen, and cerebellum.
evidence.explanation: The single p.Gln816Pro case documents caudate and putaminal atrophy alongside dystonia and seizures. Their co-occurrence does not establish which regional lesion causes either clinical manifestation or whether the basal-ganglia findings recur in other genotypes.

evidence.explanation: Published human observations; no hearing-loss subtype or frequency band is inferred.

evidence.snippet:

rule out a potential contribution of this variant to the pheno-
type although AGTPBP1 seems to be the main contributor.
evidence.explanation: The NCAPD3 co-variant is a stated confound in the first patient; it is not assumed to explain every microcephaly case.

open_questions/9.rationale: Spasticity indicates a central motor component, but the reviewed human studies do not establish the affected descending pathways. Dystonia and seizures coexist with caudate/putaminal atrophy in one case without demonstrating that this lesion causes either symptom. Hand tremor includes rest and action components, and the sporadic hearing loss is unlocalized. The broad eye-movement relation to weakness/cerebellar dysfunction is represented, while the specific origins of apraxia and esotropia are not separated. Microcephaly includes postnatal head-growth decline, but neither cerebellar loss nor peripheral motor-neuron loss alone has been shown to explain it; the first 2019 case also had a potentially contributing NCAPD3 variant. These gaps concern lesion or causal attribution, not simply absent pathway nodes.

evidence.snippet: Patient 3 presented with GDD, dysmorphic facial features “course facies, narrow forehead, thick eyebrows, broad bulbous nose, short philtrum, thick lips, and large ears,” oculomotor apraxia, and seizures.
evidence.explanation: Patient 3 carried homozygous p.Thr884Pro, classified as likely pathogenic. The distinct patient 7 carried a VUS and is not pooled as equivalent genetic evidence.

evidence.snippet: He had multiple skeletal deformities “arachnodactyly, bilateral hyperextensibility of the interphalangeal joints, bilateral low inserted thumb, toes camptodactyly, bilateral prominent heel, severe scoliosis and joint contractures” and bilateral fungal infection of both feet (Fig. 3).
evidence.explanation: The antecedent is patient 3, the likely-pathogenic AGTPBP1 case; these unusual observations remain explicitly case-scoped.

evidence.snippet: Patient 7 had a homozygous missense variant in the AGTPBP1 gene (c.1534A > G; p. (Thr512Ala) causing an amino acid change from Thr to Ala at position 512. It is classified as a variant of uncertain significance (class 3) according to the recommendations of Centogene and ACMG.
evidence.explanation: Patient 7 is genetically less certain than patient 3.

open_questions/10.rationale: The 2024 likely-pathogenic p.Thr884Pro patient had coarse facies, narrow forehead, thick eyebrows, broad bulbous nose, short philtrum, thick lips and large ears; arachnodactyly, interphalangeal hyperextensibility, low-inserted thumbs, toe camptodactyly, prominent heels, scoliosis and joint contractures were also described. Table 2 additionally records brisk reflexes, hypometric saccades and poor eye contact, and ERG showed retinal dysfunction. The extensor plantar response in the 4.5-month-old autopsy case is not separately treated as a pathological Babinski sign because that response can be physiological at this age. These are preserved as a case expansion whose individual causal attribution and recurrence are unresolved. The second AGTPBP1 patient carried p.Thr512Ala classified as a VUS and had strabismus, oculomotor apraxia, optic-nerve dysfunction and contractures; that case is not pooled as equally established genetic evidence. Mouse retinal degeneration is not substituted for these human observations.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that de novo and bi-allelic mutations in NARS1 are a significant cause of neurodevelopmental disease, where the mechanism for de novo variants could be toxic gain-of-function and for recessive variants, partial loss-of-function.
evidence.explanation: The founding series assigns partial loss of function specifically to the recessive (biallelic) alleles that define this entity, and separates it from the de novo mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Molecular modeling of the recessive c.1633C>T (p.Arg545Cys) variant shows weaker spatial positioning and tRNA selectivity.
evidence.explanation: In silico structural modelling of the recurrent recessive allele; predicted rather than measured, hence COMPUTATIONAL.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of these interactions by the R545C mutation would thus likely result in local destabilization
evidence.explanation: Structural analysis of the recurrent recessive p.Arg545Cys residue, whose side chain points away from both the dimer interface and the active site — the structural reason it destabilises locally rather than poisoning the dimer as the dominant alleles do.

steps/1.description: The initiating lesion is a pair of NARS1 alleles, in trans, that reduce but do not abolish asparaginyl-tRNA synthetase function. Reported recessive alleles include missense changes in the unique N-terminal extension (UNE-N) domain (p.Thr17Met), in the catalytic domain (p.Asp356Ala, the recurrent p.Arg545Cys), and frameshift alleles (p.Met69AspfsTer4, p.Arg386ThrfsTer19). Complete loss of the enzyme is not compatible with life, so disease-causing biallelic genotypes are necessarily partial-function rather than null. Structural modelling of p.Arg545Cys predicts weaker spatial positioning and reduced tRNA selectivity through local destabilisation near the N-terminal end of the catalytic domain.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate a reduction in NARS1 mRNA expression as well as in NARS1 enzyme levels and activity in both individual fibroblasts and induced neural progenitor cells (iNPCs).
evidence.explanation: Measures the reduction in enzyme level and activity in patient-derived cells, including a disease-relevant neural progenitor cell type.

evidence.snippet: Patient cells show reduced NARS1 protein, impaired NARS1 activity and impaired global protein synthesis.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of reduced NARS1 protein and charging activity.

evidence.snippet: As controls, we additionally assessed charging activity of three other ARSs: RARS, KARS, and TARS (for arginine, lysine, and threonine) and found patient cells had normal activity.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the aminoacylation defect is specific to NARS1 rather than a global translational-machinery failure.

steps/2.description: NARS1 is the sole enzyme that charges asparagine onto cytoplasmic tRNA-Asn. Patient fibroblasts and induced neural progenitor cells carry roughly half the normal amount of NARS1 protein and about half the normal tRNA-charging activity, and overexpression of the patient missense alleles shows the mutant proteins are unstable. The defect is specific: charging activity of the arginyl-, lysyl- and threonyl-tRNA synthetases is unaffected in the same cells, so this is not a general collapse of the translational apparatus but a targeted shortfall in one aminoacylation reaction.

evidence.snippet: Patient IPSCs showed reduced puromycin incorporation after 1 h pulse, indicating reduced protein synthesis.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of reduced global protein synthesis in patient-derived pluripotent cells.

evidence.snippet: Our findings demonstrate that NARS1 is required to meet protein synthetic needs and to support RGC proliferation in human brain development.
evidence.explanation: States the authors' conclusion linking the translational shortfall to human cortical development.

steps/3.description: Because asparagine charging is rate-limiting for any transcript containing asparagine codons, the shortfall in charged tRNA-Asn reduces bulk cytoplasmic translation. Puromycin pulse labelling of patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells shows a marked fall in incorporation into nascent protein relative to cells from unaffected parents.

evidence.snippet: Cortical brain organoid modeling shows reduced proliferation of radial glial cells (RGCs), leading to smaller organoids characteristic of microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Identifies impaired radial glial proliferation as the cellular step between the translational defect and reduced brain size.

evidence.snippet: Single-cell analysis reveals altered constituents of both astrocytic and RGC lineages, suggesting a requirement for NARS1 in RGC proliferation.
evidence.explanation: Single-cell transcriptomic support for a radial-glial-lineage-specific requirement.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest failed RGCs generation, with subsequent depletion of post-mitotic neurons
evidence.explanation: Links the progenitor defect to loss of the differentiated neuronal output, the cellular basis of a reduced cortex.

evidence.snippet: qPCR validation with cDNA from unaffected COs and affected COs at several differentiation stages, confirmed reduced CCND2 mRNA expression
evidence.explanation: Cyclin D2 is a regulator of the G1-S transition, so its reduction identifies the specific cell-cycle step behind the proliferation failure rather than leaving it unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, pseudo-time analysis showed altered cell fate towards astrocytes at the expense of neurons in affected COs
evidence.explanation: The progenitor pool is not merely smaller but differently fated, shifting towards astrocytes and away from neurons, which is why the astrocytic lineage is annotated on this node alongside radial glia.

steps/4.description: The developing cortical neuroepithelium is the tissue least able to tolerate a translational shortfall, because radial glial cells must sustain a very high biosynthetic rate through repeated rounds of division. In patient-derived cortical brain organoids, DNA synthesis is reduced, SOX2-positive neural rosettes are fewer, smaller and poorly organised, and the mature-neuron marker TUJ1 is depleted, indicating failed generation of radial glia and consequent loss of the post-mitotic neuronal output pool. Single-cell profiling shows the astrocytic and radial glial lineages are both altered.

evidence.snippet: Cleaved Caspase 3+ (CC3) cells were apparent in affected COs but barely detected in unaffected COs
evidence.explanation: The direct measurement of elevated apoptosis in patient cortical organoids, using the standard effector-caspase marker.

evidence.snippet: appeared to be a direct result of reduced cell division and increased cell death
evidence.explanation: The authors' own account of causation, naming cell death as co-equal with reduced division. This is what justifies a separate node rather than folding apoptosis into the proliferation one.

steps/5.description: Alongside reduced division, patient-derived cortical organoids show markedly elevated programmed cell death in the progenitor compartment. The founding organoid study attributes the size deficit to both routes rather than to proliferation failure alone, so the neuroepithelium is depleted by two convergent mechanisms. Modelling this as a sibling of the proliferation node keeps the two arms separable downstream.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI from the affected in 1433-III-3 showed severe microcephaly, diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, with both gray and white matter volume loss, and ventriculomegaly
evidence.explanation: The human neuroimaging correlate of the organoid proliferation defect.

evidence.snippet: All affected individuals showed microcephaly, developmental delay, and intellectual disability, with progressive loss of neurological function.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the progressive, rather than static, clinical trajectory.

steps/6.description: The depleted progenitor pool yields a small cortex, and the ongoing translational insufficiency in post-mitotic neurons superimposes a degenerative component on the developmental deficit. Brain MRI in affected individuals shows severe microcephaly with diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, loss of both grey and white matter volume, and ventriculomegaly, with milder cortical and cerebellar atrophy on scans obtained earlier in the course — the imaging signature of a process that continues after birth rather than a fixed malformation.

evidence.snippet: Peripheral neuropathy with atrophy predominantly of the distal lower limbs can be associated.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews records peripheral neuropathy as a variable associated feature of NARS1-NDD.

evidence.snippet: NCV (Nerve Conduction Velocity) showed four limbs neuropathy, neurophysiological examination performed at 2 years of age mainly sensory and demyelinating.
evidence.explanation: Electrophysiological confirmation of a demyelinating sensory neuropathy in a compound heterozygous (recessive) patient, at age two.

steps/7.description: A subset of affected individuals develop a peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy, demyelinating or axonal, with atrophy predominantly of the distal lower limbs. Nerve conduction studies can be abnormal in early childhood. Peripheral nerve is a second high-demand compartment for the same reason as the cortex — long axons and myelinating Schwann cells sustain heavy biosynthetic loads — and its involvement is what makes NARS1 disease a combined CNS/PNS disorder rather than a pure microcephaly syndrome. The peripheral arm is not universal in the recessive form and is here modelled as a parallel consequence of the same translational shortfall, not as a downstream effect of the cortical defect.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe 32 individuals from 21 families, presenting with microcephaly, neurodevelopmental delay, seizures, peripheral neuropathy, and ataxia, with de novo heterozygous and bi-allelic mutations in asparaginyl-tRNA synthetase (NARS1).
evidence.explanation: The founding cohort's summary of the combined CNS/PNS phenotype. The series pools de novo and biallelic individuals, so the sentence describes the spectrum rather than the recessive arm in isolation.

evidence.snippet: Change in muscle tone can manifest either as spasticity or as hypotonia.
evidence.explanation: Explains why the tone abnormality, and hence the gait abnormality, is bidirectional across affected individuals.

steps/8.description: The convergence of the cortical and peripheral arms produces the clinical entity: global developmental delay and impaired intellectual development with poor or absent language, progressive microcephaly, delayed walking with an ataxic and/or spastic gait, seizures, and — where the peripheral arm is present — distal weakness and abnormal nerve conduction. Muscle tone may be low or high in different individuals, which is why the gait abnormality has no single characteristic form.

evidence.snippet: Here, we identify biallelic missense and frameshift mutations in NARS1 in seven patients from three unrelated families with microcephaly and neurodevelopmental delay.
evidence.explanation: Establishes NARS1 as the causal gene for the biallelic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: There are two NARS genes: NARS1 functions in the cytoplasm while NARS2 functions in mitochondria, solely responsible for asparagine tRNA charging in these locations.
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes NARS1 from the mitochondrial paralogue NARS2, whose disorders are unrelated to this entry.

evidence.snippet: Sequence alignment of NARS1 from vertebrates showed that the residues mutated in patients were conserved across all mammals and most vertebrates.
evidence.explanation: Evolutionary conservation supporting pathogenicity of the recessive alleles.

genes/0.notes: NARS1 (chromosome 18q21.31) encodes the cytoplasmic class IIa asparaginyl-tRNA synthetase, a 548-residue obligate homodimer with a eukaryote-specific unique N-terminal extension (UNE-N), an anticodon-binding domain and a C-terminal catalytic domain. It is the only enzyme charging asparagine onto cytoplasmic tRNA-Asn; the mitochondrial reaction is carried out by the separate gene NARS2. Biallelic variants causing this disorder are distributed across the UNE-N and catalytic domains, are conserved across mammals and most vertebrates, and act by partial loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with NARS1-NDD: multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields including developmental pediatrics, speech and language therapy, neurology to manage seizures, physical therapy, orthopedics to manage scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis, nutrition/feeding, psychology to manage behavioral abnormalities, and medical genetics / genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the multidisciplinary management standard for NARS1-NDD, which includes this entity.

evidence.snippet: Currently, no disease-specific treatment exists, and symptoms are managed with supportive measures and surgeries.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that care remains supportive, with no disease-specific therapy available.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is symptom-directed and multidisciplinary, coordinating developmental paediatrics, speech and language therapy, neurology for seizure management, physical therapy, orthopaedics for scoliosis and kyphoscoliosis, nutrition and feeding support, psychology for behavioural manifestations, and medical genetics with genetic counselling. Surveillance is at each visit or as directed by the treating specialist.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with NARS1-NDD: multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields including developmental pediatrics, speech and language therapy, neurology to manage seizures, physical therapy, orthopedics to manage scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis, nutrition/feeding, psychology to manage behavioral abnormalities, and medical genetics / genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names physical therapy in the management standard.

treatments/1.description: Physical therapy addresses the gait abnormality, tone abnormality and mobility impairment, and is part of the standard multidisciplinary package.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with NARS1-NDD: multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields including developmental pediatrics, speech and language therapy, neurology to manage seizures, physical therapy, orthopedics to manage scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis, nutrition/feeding, psychology to manage behavioral abnormalities, and medical genetics / genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names speech and language therapy in the management standard.

treatments/2.description: Speech and language therapy targets the poor or absent expressive language that gives the disorder part of its name, including augmentative and alternative communication where speech does not develop.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with NARS1-NDD: multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields including developmental pediatrics, speech and language therapy, neurology to manage seizures, physical therapy, orthopedics to manage scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis, nutrition/feeding, psychology to manage behavioral abnormalities, and medical genetics / genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews assigns seizure management to neurology as part of routine care. No NARS1-specific antiseizure drug guidance exists.

treatments/3.description: Seizures are managed with standard antiseizure medication under neurology supervision. Response is heterogeneous, from seizure freedom to refractory epilepsy despite polytherapy. No agent has been shown to be preferentially effective in this genotype.

evidence.snippet: During follow-up we highlighted: dysphagia (which became increasingly severe until it became incompatible with oral feeding, with gastrostomy implantation, resulting in resolution of feeding difficulties), strabismus, hypotonia.
evidence.explanation: Documents gastrostomy resolving the feeding difficulty in a biallelic patient.

treatments/4.description: Where dysphagia becomes incompatible with oral feeding, gastrostomy resolves the feeding difficulty. Nutrition and feeding support is a named component of routine care.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with NARS1-NDD: multidisciplinary care by specialists in relevant fields including developmental pediatrics, speech and language therapy, neurology to manage seizures, physical therapy, orthopedics to manage scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis, nutrition/feeding, psychology to manage behavioral abnormalities, and medical genetics / genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews assigns scoliosis and kyphoscoliosis management to orthopaedics as part of routine care.

treatments/5.description: Scoliosis and kyphoscoliosis develop as secondary neuromuscular complications and are managed by orthopaedics, surgically where indicated. GeneReviews names orthopaedic input for these specifically rather than folding it into general supportive care.

evidence.snippet: Carrier testing for at-risk relatives requires prior identification of the NARS1 pathogenic variants in the family.
evidence.explanation: States the precondition for cascade carrier testing.

evidence.snippet: Once the NARS1 pathogenic variant(s) have been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: States the reproductive options counselling must cover.

treatments/6.description: Counselling covers the 25% per-pregnancy recurrence risk for carrier couples, the unaffected status of heterozygous siblings, and the availability of prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing once the familial variant pair is known. Carrier testing of at-risk relatives requires prior identification of the familial variants.

evidence.snippet: Asparagine supplementation completely restored cell proliferation defects in patient-derived fibroblasts and prevented activation of the ISR.
evidence.explanation: The rescue result. PARTIAL for this entity because the alleles tested were dominant nonsense variants, not the biallelic hypomorphic alleles curated here.

evidence.snippet: We found that two dominant NARS1 nonsense alleles, R534X and R522X, cause a cytotoxic phenotype and elicit the integrated stress response (ISR).
evidence.explanation: Identifies exactly which alleles were tested, which is what limits the result's transfer to the recessive entity.

evidence.snippet: Asparagine supplementation may be not effective in controlling the seizures in asparagine synthetase deficiency, and it is likely to make them worse.
evidence.explanation: A safety counterpoint by analogy, not a result in this disorder. The one human report of asparagine supplementation in the closest clinical phenocopy, where the substrate is genuinely depleted and supplementation therefore has the stronger rationale, describes worsening seizures requiring discontinuation. Since seizures are frequent in this entity too, any trial of supplementation here has to anticipate that signal. REFUTE is recorded against the therapeutic proposition, with the caveat that the disorder studied is asparagine synthetase deficiency rather than NARS1 disease.

open_questions/0.rationale: A 2026 study built a human cell system for pathogenic NARS1 alleles and found that asparagine supplementation completely restored proliferation in patient-derived fibroblasts and prevented integrated stress response activation, with cognate tRNA supplementation and a GCN2 inhibitor giving partial benefit. This is the first credible disease-modifying strategy for any NARS1 genotype and is mechanistically plausible for the recessive form, since raising substrate availability should partially compensate a hypomorphic enzyme. Two things keep this an open hypothesis rather than a curated treatment. First, scope: the alleles tested were the dominant nonsense variants R534X and R522X, which act by dominant-negative poisoning, not the hypomorphic biallelic alleles that define this entity, and whether substrate supplementation helps when the defect is reduced enzyme abundance rather than a poisoned dimer has not been shown. Second, a safety signal from the nearest clinical analogue: in asparagine synthetase deficiency, where asparagine really is depleted and the rationale for replacing it is stronger, the single reported human trial of supplementation was followed by irritability, sleep disturbance and worsening seizures, and had to be stopped. No clinical trial exists in any NARS1 genotype. A separate, related open question is whether circulating and CSF asparagine are in fact normal in NARS1 disease; that is widely assumed from the mechanism but has not been measured in a NARS1 cohort, and it matters both for the therapeutic rationale and for using asparagine as the discriminator against the ASNS phenocopy.

evidence.snippet: Similarly, the homozygous knock-in mouse model (p.Ser461Phe/Ser472Phe in mouse) also demonstrated loss-of-function characteristics.
evidence.explanation: The only published mammalian NARS1 knock-in carries a dominant neuropathy allele, not a recessive neurodevelopmental one; PARTIAL because it evidences the absence of a matched model rather than the disorder itself.

evidence.snippet: Cortical brain organoid modeling shows reduced proliferation of radial glial cells (RGCs), leading to smaller organoids characteristic of microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: The available model covers the developmental arm only, which is what leaves the degenerative and peripheral arms unmodelled.

open_questions/1.rationale: The disorder's flagship model is a patient-derived cortical organoid, which recapitulates the developmental progenitor-proliferation defect with high fidelity but stops at fetal corticogenesis. It cannot model the postnatal neurodegenerative course, the peripheral neuropathy, or the seizures — precisely the features that make this a combined CNS/PNS degenerative disorder rather than a static microcephaly. The one published mammalian in vivo NARS1 model is a knock-in of the dominant p.Ser461Phe neuropathy allele, which models the wrong entity. Curators should not treat organoid evidence as covering the degenerative or peripheral arms, and the mechanism_confidence on the peripheral node is PROVISIONAL for this reason.

evidence.snippet: Other DysmorphismMaxillary hypoplasia, progeroid features, arachnodactylyProgeroid appearance, arachnodactylyProgeroid features, arachnodactylyArachnodactyly, cubitus valgus, pes planovalgusArachnodactyly, cubitus valgus, pes planovalgus
evidence.explanation: The per-family dysmorphism pattern that hints at genotype-linked features while being far too small to establish one.

open_questions/2.rationale: Clinical variability within the recessive form is wide — tone may be low or high, seizures may be absent or refractory, neuropathy is present in only a subset — yet no genotype-phenotype correlation has been established. Some findings do track with family and genotype in the founding series (progeroid features in the p.Thr17Met siblings, cataracts in the p.Arg545Cys homozygotes), but with three families and seven individuals these are observations, not correlations. Because the total reported biallelic population is small, resolving this requires an international registry rather than another single-family report.

evidence.snippet: It encodes a putative transmembrane protein.
evidence.explanation: The gene-discovery paper reports that CLN8 encodes a transmembrane protein.

evidence.snippet: CLN8 is an ER to Golgi cargo receptor that is required for lysosomal biogenesis
evidence.explanation: Establishes the ER-to-Golgi cargo-receptor role of CLN8 in lysosomal biogenesis, based on mouse studies.

evidence.snippet: We show that CLN8 catalyzes the essential step in the biosynthesis of bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate, a phospholipid critical for lysosome function.
evidence.explanation: Recent biochemical work links CLN8 directly to lysosomal membrane lipid homeostasis via bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate synthesis.

steps/1.description: CLN8 encodes a multipass transmembrane protein of the TRAM-LAG1-CLN8 (TLC) domain family that resides in the endoplasmic reticulum and ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, where it functions as an ER-to-Golgi cargo receptor delivering soluble lysosomal enzymes and participates in membrane phospholipid remodeling. Loss of CLN8 function impairs lysosomal enzyme trafficking and lipid homeostasis, initiating the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis disease process.

evidence.snippet: The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs) are a genetically heterogeneous group of progressive neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment in various tissues.
evidence.explanation: Defines the accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment as the hallmark pathology of the NCLs, of which Northern epilepsy (CLN8) is a subtype.

evidence.snippet: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs) are a group of rare, inherited, neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disorders that affect children and adults.
evidence.explanation: Classifies the NCLs, including CLN8/Northern epilepsy, as lysosomal storage disorders.

steps/2.description: Like other neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, Northern epilepsy is characterized by intraneuronal accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid lipopigment; progressive storage contributes to neuronal dysfunction and slow neurodegeneration.

edges/1.description: CLN8 dysfunction is part of the NCL pathway that produces abnormal lysosomal storage material.

evidence.snippet: Here we report the positional cloning of a novel gene, CLN8, which is mutated in EPMR.
evidence.explanation: This is the primary report identifying CLN8 as the gene mutated in EPMR / Northern epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: EPMR patients were homozygous for a missense mutation (70C-->G, R24G) that was not found in homozygosity in 433 controls.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the homozygous CLN8 founder missense variant (c.70C>G, R24G) in EPMR / Northern epilepsy patients.

evidence.snippet: Phenotypic divergence is exemplified by different CLN8 mutations giving rise to two very different diseases, the mild CLN8 disease, EPMR (progressive epilepsy with mental retardation), and the more severe CLN8 disease, late infantile variant.
evidence.explanation: Documents CLN8 allelic heterogeneity: the mild EPMR/Northern epilepsy phenotype versus the severe late-infantile variant.

genes/0.notes: Northern epilepsy is caused by biallelic CLN8 variants. In Finland virtually all patients are homozygous for the founder missense variant c.70C>G (p.Arg24Gly / R24G). CLN8 is a member of the TRAM-LAG1-CLN8 (TLC) domain protein family and is allelic with the more severe late-infantile variant CLN8 disease.

evidence.snippet: Clonazepam and sodium valproate had some antiepileptic effect, clonazepam being the more beneficial of the two.
evidence.explanation: Documents the partial antiepileptic benefit of anticonvulsant therapy (clonazepam and sodium valproate) reported in Northern epilepsy patients.

treatments/0.description: Management of Northern epilepsy is symptomatic and centered on seizure control; there is no CLN8-specific disease-modifying therapy. Historically, clonazepam and sodium valproate provided partial antiepileptic benefit.

evidence.snippet: A (GCG)6 repeat encoding a polyalanine tract located at the N terminus of the protein was expanded to (GCG)8-13 in the 144 OPMD families screened.
evidence.explanation: The founding genetic study identifying the expanded polyalanine-encoding repeat in PABPN1 (then PABP2) across 144 OPMD families.

evidence.snippet: The mutations cause the lengthening of an N-terminal polyalanine domain.
evidence.explanation: States the protein-level consequence of the repeat expansion that defines this node. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

evidence.snippet: This gene encodes the poly(A) binding protein 2 (PABP2), an abundant nuclear protein that binds with high affinity to nascent poly(A) tails, stimulating their extension and controlling their length.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the normal nuclear poly(A)-binding and polyadenylation-control function of the mutated protein, grounding the molecular-function and biological-process bindings on this node.

steps/1.description: A short GCN (GCG) trinucleotide repeat in the first exon of PABPN1 expands from the normal (GCG)6 to (GCG)8-13, lengthening the N-terminal polyalanine tract of the nuclear poly(A)-binding protein. PABPN1 normally binds nascent poly(A) tails with high affinity and controls their extension and length, so the lesion falls on a protein with a defined nuclear RNA-processing role.

evidence.snippet: This suggests that the polyalanine expansions in PABP2 induce a misfolding and aggregation of the protein into insoluble inclusions, similarly to events in neurodegenerative diseases caused by CAG/polyglutamine expansions.
evidence.explanation: States the misfolding-and-aggregation mechanism this node models, and situates it alongside the polyglutamine proteotoxicity diseases.

evidence.snippet: In this work we report that PABP2 is detected in filamentous nuclear inclusions, which are the pathological hallmark of OPMD.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the aggregating species inside the hallmark inclusions as PABPN1 itself.

evidence.snippet: Typical tubulofilamentous intranuclear inclusions (INI) of 8.5 nm outer diameter were present in all cases.
evidence.explanation: Electron-microscopic characterisation of the inclusion ultrastructure and calibre quoted in this node's description.

evidence.snippet: This indicates that the expression of Ala-expanded-PABPN1 causes the formation of nuclear aggregates before the onset of muscle weakness.
evidence.explanation: Places aggregation causally upstream of clinical weakness by demonstrating it in presymptomatic carriers.

steps/2.description: Expanded PABPN1 misfolds and self-associates into insoluble, tubulofilamentous intranuclear inclusions roughly 8.5 nm in outer diameter within skeletal muscle fibre nuclei. These inclusions are the pathological hallmark of OPMD, are decorated by anti-PABPN1 antibodies, and contain a salt-extraction-resistant form of the protein. They appear in muscle biopsies of presymptomatic Ala-expanded PABPN1 carriers, placing aggregation upstream of clinical weakness.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the inclusions were labeled with antibodies directed against ubiquitin and the subunits of the proteasome and contained a form of PABP2 that was more resistant to salt extraction than the protein dispersed in the nucleoplasm.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates co-sequestration of ubiquitin and proteasome subunits within the inclusions, and the insolubility of the trapped PABPN1.

evidence.snippet: The INIs also contain ubiquitin, proteasome subunits, HSP 40, HSP 70, SKIP, and abundant poly(A)-mRNA.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the sequestered proteostasis components and RNA cargo listed in this node. Evidence source is OTHER because this is a review.

steps/3.description: The intranuclear inclusions trap poly(A) mRNA together with ubiquitin, proteasome subunits and the chaperones HSP40 and HSP70. Sequestering both the RNA cargo of PABPN1 and the machinery that would normally clear misfolded protein is the proposed route by which aggregation becomes toxic, potentially interfering with nuclear export of poly(A) RNA.

evidence.snippet: On immunohistochemistry for anti-PABPN1 in OPMD, PABPN1-positive aggregates were observed in the myonuclei, corresponding to the p62 positive myo-INIs
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the aggregates burdening OPMD myonuclei are PABPN1-positive, tying the tissue-level lesion to the upstream molecular node.

evidence.snippet: the myo-INIs were found in all of the patients (100%, 15/15)
evidence.explanation: Establishes that intranuclear inclusions are present in every OPMD muscle biopsy in this series, supporting the high myonuclear burden described.

evidence.snippet: Unique nuclear filament inclusions in skeletal muscle fibres are its pathological hallmark.
evidence.explanation: Locates the defining lesion in skeletal muscle fibres, the cell type bound on this node.

steps/4.description: Progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle fibres with rimmed vacuoles and myopathic change, selectively and earliest affecting the levator palpebrae and pharyngeal musculature and later the limb girdles, predominantly proximally and in the lower limbs. In OPMD roughly one in eight myonuclei carries a p62-positive intranuclear inclusion, a far higher burden than in other rimmed-vacuolar myopathies.

evidence.snippet: Ptosis was the first reported symptom in two-thirds of the patients, and half of the subjects studied had evidence of ophthalmoplegia.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies ptosis as the presenting symptom in a genotyped UK OPMD cohort.

evidence.snippet: the mean age of onset of ptosis is usually 48 years and of dysphagia 50 years
evidence.explanation: Supports the adult age of onset stated in this phenotype's description.

steps/5.description: Progressive, usually bilateral drooping of the eyelids from levator palpebrae involvement. It is the first reported symptom in about two-thirds of patients and has a mean age of onset around 48 years.

evidence.snippet: Swallowing difficulties, which determine prognosis, increase the risk for potentially life-threatening aspiration pneumonia and poor nutrition.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the prognostic weight of dysphagia and its two principal complications.

steps/6.description: Progressive oropharyngeal swallowing difficulty with a mean onset around age 50. Dysphagia determines prognosis in OPMD because it drives aspiration pneumonia and malnutrition.

evidence.snippet: In addition to the characteristic OPMD symptoms including ptosis and dysphagia, other symptoms such as limb girdle and axial weakness, and external ophthalmoplegia were frequently observed.
evidence.explanation: Reports limb girdle weakness as a frequent finding in a nationwide Dutch OPMD cohort.

steps/5.description: The initiating event in osteonecrosis is disruption of the blood supply to bone. This may be mechanical (traumatic vessel disruption after fracture/dislocation), occlusive (sickled erythrocytes, nitrogen gas emboli, thrombosis), or the result of glucocorticoid- and alcohol-induced endothelial dysfunction, coagulopathy, and hypofibrinolysis. Across non-traumatic etiologies, endothelial dysfunction within a chronic inflammatory milieu produces thrombosis, coagulopathy, and poor angiogenesis, preventing effective repair and revascularization of bone lesions.

steps/8.description: Disrupted perfusion, lipotoxic stress, and failed revascularization cause ischemic death (apoptosis and necrosis) of osteocytes and bone marrow cells in the subchondral region. The necrotic segment cannot remodel normally, setting the stage for structural failure.

steps/9.description: Accumulated necrotic bone weakens the subchondral region. Under continued weight-bearing load, a subchondral fracture develops and the articular surface progressively collapses. Without effective early intervention, a high proportion of femoral heads progress to collapse, and end-stage disease produces secondary osteoarthritis requiring total hip arthroplasty.

open_questions/0.rationale: The gut-bone axis in AVN is assembled entirely from indirect evidence. Human data are cross-sectional microbiota-metabolome signatures, which cannot order dysbiosis and disease in time; reversal of pathological change is shown in animals rather than patients; and the causal claim rests on Mendelian randomization, which supports a contribution of selected taxa without identifying the intermediate steps. The proposed route runs dysbiosis → reduced SCFA → epithelial barrier dysfunction → immune activation → vascular endothelial injury, feeding "Vascular supply disruption", with dysbiosis-mediated metabolic dysregulation potentially compounding lipotoxicity. Glucocorticoid exposure and heavy alcohol are established causes of AVN in this entry and are also causes of dysbiosis, so confounding by shared driver is the live alternative to a gut-bone pathway. Resolving this decides whether the two influences_mechanisms edges recorded here are mechanism or correlation, and whether microbiota-targeted intervention is worth pursuing in AVN at all.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, our results show that the strategy of pooling DNA is a powerful, cost-effective application for WES in consanguineous families and establish PAX1 as a new disease-causing gene for OFCS and as part of the EYA-DACH-SIX-PAX network, important in early embryogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes PAX1 causality and places it in the PAX-SIX-EYA-DACH network shared with EYA1.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrated that these mutant PAX1 proteins have an altered conformation and flexibility of the paired box domain and reduced transcriptional activity.
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms reduced transcriptional activity across a further set of patient alleles.

evidence.snippet: Mechanically, PAX1 competes with SUMO E3 ligase PIASy to bind to TCF7L2, thus perturbing TCF7L2 SUMOylation level, further reducing its transcriptional activity and protein stability.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the molecular mechanism by which PAX1 acts, competition with PIASy for TCF7L2 binding, which is what the disease alleles disrupt.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, our data show PAX1 mutations found in SCID patients significantly compromise the suppressing ability of PAX1 on Wnt signaling.
evidence.explanation: Connects the patient alleles specifically to loss of Wnt repression, making this the proximate molecular defect.

steps/1.description: Biallelic PAX1 variants abolish or reduce the DNA-binding and transcriptional activity of a paired-box transcription factor. Both mechanisms are documented: hypofunctional missense alleles in the conserved paired-box domain reduce transactivation of PAX1 target promoters, while frameshift and nonsense alleles remove the protein. PAX1 sits within the PAX-SIX-EYA-DACH network that also contains EYA1 and SIX1, which is why the PAX1 and EYA1 disorders share a branchial-arch phenotype despite differing in inheritance and in the thymic component.

evidence.snippet: The mouse model strongly supports the hypothesis that PAX1 depletion in our patients caused thymus aplasia responsible for SCID.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the immunodeficiency to thymic aplasia rather than an intrinsic lymphocyte defect.

steps/2.description: Failure of the PAX1-dependent transcriptional programme in the third pharyngeal pouch produces thymic aplasia or hypoplasia. The lesion is in the thymic epithelial stroma, not in the haematopoietic progenitors that would normally seed it.

evidence.snippet: We investigated the molecular and cellular basis of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) in six patients with otofaciocervical syndrome type 2 who failed to attain T cell reconstitution after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, despite successful engraftment in three of them.
evidence.explanation: The engraftment-without-reconstitution result is the direct clinical demonstration that the defect is stromal rather than haematopoietic.

evidence.snippet: Normal ex vivo differentiation of PAX1-deficient CD34+ cells into mature T cells demonstrated the absence of a hematopoietic cell-intrinsic defect.
evidence.explanation: Directly excludes a haematopoietic-intrinsic defect by showing patient CD34+ cells differentiate normally outside the patient's thymus, which localises the lesion to the stroma.

steps/3.description: Absent or severely reduced T cell output producing a syndromic severe combined immunodeficiency. The stromal locus of the defect is therapeutically decisive: allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation supplies progenitors but not the epithelial niche they require, so T cell reconstitution fails even after successful engraftment.

evidence.snippet: Experimentally, mice with PAX1 deficiency showed vertebral column anomalies and different degrees of thymic hypoplasia
evidence.explanation: The mouse phenotype pairs vertebral and thymic involvement, matching the two human expression domains.

steps/4.description: Loss of PAX1 in the sclerotome disrupts vertebral column and shoulder girdle development, producing the vertebral anomalies, sloping shoulders and winged, hypoplastic scapulae that give the syndrome its name.

evidence.snippet: shoulder girdle anomalies (sloping shoulders, low-set clavicles, winged scapulae, and trapezius hypoplasia)
evidence.explanation: Describes the shoulder girdle anomaly complex including scapular winging.

steps/5.description: Winged, low and laterally set scapulae with sloping shoulders and trapezius hypoplasia — the shoulder girdle anomaly that names the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The major clinical features of OTFCS include ear malformations (external/middle/inner ear), facial dysmorphism, shoulder girdle abnormalities, vertebral anomalies, and mild intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Lists vertebral anomalies among the major clinical features.

steps/6.description: Segmentation and morphological anomalies of the vertebral column.

evidence.snippet: The mouse model strongly supports the hypothesis that PAX1 depletion in our patients caused thymus aplasia responsible for SCID.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the immunodeficiency to thymic aplasia. This is the paper's own mouse-model inference, so it is graded MODEL_ORGANISM and does not stand alone for this human phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The most severe cases displayed a T−B+NK+ severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)-like phenotype secondary to thymic aplasia due to impaired differentiation of thymic epithelial cells
evidence.explanation: Direct human evidence for thymic aplasia in PAX1-deficient patients, and it names the epithelial differentiation defect that causes it.

evidence.snippet: Thymic aplasia and hypoplasia were associated with impaired T cell immunity.
evidence.explanation: Reports both the aplastic and hypoplastic ends of the thymic phenotype in the patient cohort.

steps/7.description: Absent or severely hypoplastic thymus, the feature that separates OTFCS2 from every other otofaciocervical phenotype.

evidence.snippet: These results identify biallelic, loss-of-function PAX1 mutations as the cause of a syndromic form of SCID due to altered thymus development.
evidence.explanation: Establishes syndromic SCID as a consequence of biallelic PAX1 loss.

evidence.snippet: However, more severe expanded features, including thymus aplasia, T-cell immunodeficiency, and recurrent infections, were observed in other successive studies
evidence.explanation: Places the immunodeficiency as a feature of some but not all reported families. Graded PARTIAL because this paper's own patient lacked immunodeficiency, so it supports variable rather than constant expression.

steps/8.description: Syndromic SCID from failed thymic T cell development. Severity varies: at least one biallelic truncating genotype has been reported without immunodeficiency.

evidence.snippet: However, more severe expanded features, including thymus aplasia, T-cell immunodeficiency, and recurrent infections, were observed in other successive studies
evidence.explanation: Reports recurrent infections among the severe end of the reported spectrum.

steps/9.description: Recurrent infection secondary to T cell deficiency.

evidence.snippet: New overlapping features with DiGeorge syndrome included primary hypoparathyroidism (n = 5) and congenital heart defects (n = 2), in line with PAX1 expression during early embryogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Reports primary hypoparathyroidism in five of six patients in the cohort that first characterised it in PAX1 deficiency.

steps/10.description: Primary hypoparathyroidism from failed parathyroid development, a third/fourth pharyngeal pouch derivative like the thymus. Recognised only recently as part of the PAX1 phenotype and one of the features that makes the syndrome DiGeorge-like.

evidence.snippet: New overlapping features with DiGeorge syndrome included primary hypoparathyroidism (n = 5) and congenital heart defects (n = 2), in line with PAX1 expression during early embryogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Reports congenital heart defects in two of six patients.

steps/11.description: Congenital cardiac malformation, part of the DiGeorge-like pharyngeal field phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We generated patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and differentiated them into thymic epithelial progenitor cells and found that they have an altered transcriptional profile, including for genes involved in the development of the thymus and other tissues derived from pharyngeal pouches.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived cells show the transcriptional consequence directly in the relevant lineage.

edges/1.description: PAX1 directly drives the transcriptional programme of pharyngeal pouch-derived tissue, of which the thymic epithelium is the principal product.

evidence.snippet: PAX1 encodes a transcription factor protein specifically expressed during the development of the skeleton, thymus, and parathyroid glands
evidence.explanation: States the expression domains that partition the phenotype into skeletal and thymic components.

edges/2.description: PAX1 is expressed in the sclerotome and is required for vertebral column and shoulder girdle patterning, the non-immune half of the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The most severe cases displayed a T−B+NK+ severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)-like phenotype secondary to thymic aplasia due to impaired differentiation of thymic epithelial cells
evidence.explanation: States the epithelial differentiation defect as the cause of the thymic aplasia.

edges/3.description: Failure of the PAX1-dependent pharyngeal pouch programme is what leaves the thymus absent or hypoplastic.

evidence.snippet: New overlapping features with DiGeorge syndrome included primary hypoparathyroidism (n = 5) and congenital heart defects (n = 2), in line with PAX1 expression during early embryogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the hypoparathyroidism to PAX1 expression during early embryogenesis, the same developmental window as the thymic defect.

edges/4.description: The parathyroid glands derive from the same third and fourth pharyngeal pouches as the thymus, so the same field defect produces hypoparathyroidism.

evidence.snippet: New overlapping features with DiGeorge syndrome included primary hypoparathyroidism (n = 5) and congenital heart defects (n = 2), in line with PAX1 expression during early embryogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Reports the association in two of six patients. Graded PARTIAL because the paper establishes co-occurrence and a plausible developmental window rather than a mechanism.

edges/5.description: Cardiac malformation accompanies the pharyngeal field defect, as it does in DiGeorge syndrome, but the intermediate steps from PAX1 loss to the cardiac phenotype have not been established.

evidence.snippet: These results identify biallelic, loss-of-function PAX1 mutations as the cause of a syndromic form of SCID due to altered thymus development.
evidence.explanation: States the causal chain from PAX1 loss through thymus development to SCID.

edges/6.description: Without thymic epithelium there is no niche for T cell development, so T cells fail to mature regardless of progenitor availability.

evidence.snippet: These results identify biallelic, loss-of-function PAX1 mutations as the cause of a syndromic form of SCID due to altered thymus development.
evidence.explanation: States the causal chain from altered thymus development to SCID.

edges/7.description: Absent thymic T cell output is the immunodeficiency.

evidence.snippet: However, more severe expanded features, including thymus aplasia, T-cell immunodeficiency, and recurrent infections, were observed in other successive studies
evidence.explanation: Places recurrent infections downstream of the T-cell immunodeficiency in the severe end of the spectrum.

edges/8.description: Absent T cell immunity produces recurrent infection.

evidence.snippet: Experimentally, mice with PAX1 deficiency showed vertebral column anomalies and different degrees of thymic hypoplasia
evidence.explanation: Links PAX1 deficiency directly to vertebral column anomalies.

edges/9.description: Sclerotome-derived vertebral patterning fails, producing the segmentation and morphological anomalies of the spine.

evidence.snippet: shoulder girdle anomalies (sloping shoulders, low-set clavicles, winged scapulae, and trapezius hypoplasia)
evidence.explanation: Documents the shoulder girdle anomaly complex. Graded INDIRECT because it establishes the phenotype without demonstrating the sclerotome route to it.

edges/10.description: The shoulder girdle anomalies accompany the axial skeletal defect, but the specific requirement for PAX1 in scapular and clavicular patterning has not been separately demonstrated.

evidence.snippet: Filtering for variants with a percentage of alternate reads ≥ 90 % and a coverage of at least five reads identified only a single novel homozygous variant, c.497G>T, located in PAX1 that co-segregated with the disease in the family.
evidence.explanation: Cosegregation of the homozygous PAX1 variant in a large consanguineous family establishes causality.

evidence.snippet: We identified rare biallelic PAX1 rare variants in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Confirms biallelic PAX1 variants across an independent six-patient cohort.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic PAX1 variants cause otofaciocervical syndrome type 2. Reported alleles include the hypofunctional paired-box missense p.G166V, nonsense alleles and frameshift insertions. PAX1 lies at 20p11.22 and encodes a 534-amino-acid paired-box transcription factor whose conserved 128-residue paired domain carries the DNA-binding activity.

evidence.snippet: Corrective treatment was required in 4/6 patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that corrective immune therapy is needed in the majority of reported patients.

evidence.snippet: This group of disorders cannot be corrected by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, but upon timely recognition as thymic defects, can successfully be treated by thymus transplantation using cultured postnatal thymic tissue with the generation of naïve T-cells showing a diverse repertoire.
evidence.explanation: States both the failure of HSCT and the success of cultured thymus tissue for this class of disorder, of which OTFCS2 is named a member.

evidence.snippet: Immune reconstitution after the current treatment is usually incomplete with relatively common inflammatory and autoimmune complications, emphasizing the importance for improving strategies for thymus replacement therapy
evidence.explanation: Qualifies the benefit: reconstitution is usually incomplete and carries inflammatory and autoimmune complications. Graded PARTIAL because it tempers rather than supports the therapy's efficacy.

evidence.snippet: Our aims were to study 105 patients treated with cultured thymus tissue (CTT), and in this report, to focus on the outcomes of 95 patients with treatment-naive congenital athymia.
evidence.explanation: The outcome dataset for this therapy, 105 treated children. Graded PARTIAL because the cohort is congenital athymia of all causes rather than PAX1 deficiency specifically, so it establishes the therapy's track record rather than its effect in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Currently, there are no approved therapies to treat congenital athymia, a condition of immune deficiency resulting in high early mortality due to infection and immune dysregulation.
evidence.explanation: States the clinical stakes - congenital athymia is untreated by any approved therapy and carries high early mortality - which is why timely recognition matters. Graded PARTIAL because it establishes the need for this therapy rather than supporting its efficacy, and sits on the very treatment it says is unapproved.

treatments/0.description: Transplantation of cultured allogeneic thymus tissue supplies the epithelial niche that PAX1-deficient patients lack, and is the rational corrective therapy for the immunodeficiency. Reported PAX1-deficient patients recovered T cell immunity substantially better after thymus transplantation than after allogeneic HSCT. This is the same approach used for congenital athymia in complete DiGeorge syndrome and FOXN1 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation resulted in poor immune reconstitution with absent naïve T cells, contrasting with the superior recovery of T cell immunity after thymus transplantation.
evidence.explanation: Directly contrasts the two interventions against the same node and establishes thymus transplantation as the one that works.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces the missing thymic epithelial niche so that the patient's own normal haematopoietic progenitors can complete T cell development.

evidence.snippet: New overlapping features with DiGeorge syndrome included primary hypoparathyroidism (n = 5) and congenital heart defects (n = 2), in line with PAX1 expression during early embryogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the hypoparathyroidism that this management addresses. Graded PARTIAL because the paper documents the endocrine phenotype without reporting the replacement regimen or its outcome.

treatments/1.description: Calcium and active vitamin D replacement for the primary hypoparathyroidism, which is present in most reported patients and required corrective treatment in the majority of the characterised cohort. Curated as standard management of the curated hypoparathyroidism phenotype rather than as a PAX1-specific therapy.

evidence.snippet: We investigated the molecular and cellular basis of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) in six patients with otofaciocervical syndrome type 2 who failed to attain T cell reconstitution after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, despite successful engraftment in three of them.
evidence.explanation: Refutes HSCT as effective therapy for the T cell defect in this disease; graded REFUTE because the outcome measured was failure of the intervention to achieve its goal.

treatments/2.description: Allogeneic HSCT has been attempted for the immunodeficiency but does not restore T cell immunity in PAX1 deficiency, because the block is in the thymic epithelial niche rather than in the haematopoietic progenitors. Reported patients failed T cell reconstitution despite successful donor engraftment. Recorded here as a documented therapeutic failure, which is itself clinically actionable.

evidence.snippet: Homozygous truncating mutations were identified in ERCC6L2 in two of the individuals. Both of these mutations affect the subcellular localization and stability of ERCC6L2.
evidence.explanation: The discovery paper shows that the variants destabilise and mislocalise the protein, so the mechanism is loss of function rather than a dominant effect.

steps/2.description: Biallelic truncating variants at or upstream of the helicase domain remove the protein's function and, for the originally described alleles, its subcellular localisation and stability.

evidence.snippet: We confirm that ERCC6L2 patients' lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) are hypersensitive to DNA-damaging agents that specifically activate the transcription coupled nucleotide excision repair (TCNER) pathway.
evidence.explanation: The pathway specificity of the sensitivity is what localises the defect to transcription-coupled repair rather than to repair in general.

evidence.snippet: Using affinity-based mass spectrometry we found that ERCC6L2 interacts with DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK), a regulatory component of the RNA Pol II transcription complex.
evidence.explanation: The physical interaction supplies the molecular route from the gene to the transcription machinery.

steps/3.description: Patient cells are hypersensitive to agents that specifically activate transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, and also to transcription inhibitors that interfere with RNA Pol II, with an abnormally delayed transcription recovery. ERCC6L2 interacts with DNA-PK, a regulatory component of the RNA Pol II transcription complex.

evidence.snippet: Sustained replication stress and DNA damage in Ercc6l2-deficient HSPCs cause p53 pathway activation followed by cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.
evidence.explanation: The step from replication stress to p53 activation is stated as the measured causal sequence.

steps/4.description: Sustained replication stress and DNA damage in haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. The haematopoietic restriction of a ubiquitously expressed repair gene is not fully explained.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, Ercc6l2 deficiency results in decreased expression of master hematopoietic regulators Runx1 and Gata1 in HSPCs.
evidence.explanation: A second, p53-independent contribution to the haematopoietic failure.

steps/5.description: p53 activation drives cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, and Ercc6l2 deficiency also lowers expression of the master haematopoietic regulators Runx1 and Gata1. The result is fewer stem and progenitor cells.

evidence.snippet: This observation was confirmed by CIBERSORTx RNA-sequencing deconvolution performed on ERCC6L2-silenced erythroid-committed cells, which demonstrated higher proportions of polychromatic erythroblasts and reduced orthochromatic erythroblasts versus controls.
evidence.explanation: The maturation block is localised to a specific step in erythroid differentiation.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that the consequences of ERCC6L2-deficiency are not limited to HSPCs, as we observe a striking phenotype in patient-derived and ERCC6L2-silenced MSCs, which exhibit enhanced osteogenesis and suppressed adipogenesis
evidence.explanation: The niche phenotype is measured in patient-derived stromal cells, so the disease is not purely stem-cell intrinsic.

steps/6.description: Delayed erythroid differentiation with a shift toward polychromatic and away from orthochromatic erythroblasts. The stromal compartment is also affected: patient-derived mesenchymal stromal cells show enhanced osteogenesis and suppressed adipogenesis, so the niche is remodelled as well as the stem cell.

evidence.snippet: Changes in the complete blood count were mild despite severe bone marrow (BM) hypoplasia and somatic TP53 mutations, with no significant difference between subjects with or without HMs.
evidence.explanation: Severe hypoplasia with mild count changes is measured across the cohort.

steps/7.description: Severe marrow hypoplasia. Peripheral counts understate it, which is why the diagnosis is often delayed and why active surveillance rather than count monitoring is what the literature recommends.

evidence.snippet: However, p53 loss fails to normalize replication stress, allowing for the accumulation of DNA damage over time, which increases the likelihood for leukemic transformation.
evidence.explanation: The rescue is partial in exactly the way that matters: fitness is restored, the underlying lesion is not.

steps/8.description: Somatic TP53 mutation restores the fitness of the ERCC6L2-deficient stem cell and corrects the marrow failure. It does not correct the replication stress, so DNA damage keeps accumulating in a clone that can no longer arrest or die. This is the pivot of the whole disease.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic germ line excision repair cross-complementing 6 like 2 (ERCC6L2) variants strongly predispose to bone marrow failure (BMF) and myeloid malignancies, characterized by somatic TP53-mutated clones and erythroid predominance.
evidence.explanation: The malignancy's defining molecular and morphological features are stated for the whole cohort.

evidence.snippet: Monosomy 7 was also described in 7/10 patients with MDS/AML.
evidence.explanation: A second recurrent cytogenetic lesion in the transformed clone, present in the same proportion as the TP53 mutations.

steps/9.description: Myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia with somatic TP53 mutations and erythroid predominance. Three-year overall survival falls to 19% once this develops.

evidence.snippet: We present two unrelated adolescent females with unexplained prolonged bicytopenia, unremarkable medical history and normal physical findings who were diagnosed with a rare non-classical ERCC6L2-associatedIBMFS.
evidence.explanation: A bicytopenic, otherwise normal presentation is what makes the frequency band FREQUENT rather than VERY_FREQUENT for true pancytopenia.

steps/10.description: Cytopenias are usually mild relative to the marrow findings, and can present as isolated or bilineage rather than trilineage loss. Two adolescents presented with unexplained prolonged bicytopenia and nothing else.

evidence.snippet: Most patients presented with trilineage cytopenia
evidence.explanation: Thrombocytopenia is named first among the trilineage cytopenias present in most patients, with the range of presenting values.

evidence.snippet: Most patients presented with trilineage cytopenia
evidence.explanation: Anemia is one of the three cytopenias present in most patients.

evidence.snippet: 7 g/dL), and neutropenia (between 100 and 1600/μL).
evidence.explanation: Completes the trilineage cytopenia sentence, with the presenting neutrophil range.

evidence.snippet: In summary, approximately a third of the whole cohort of patients (10/31) developed MDS or AML.
evidence.explanation: 10 of 31 is 32%, which maps to FREQUENT, and the sentence names MDS explicitly rather than leaving it to be inferred from a malignancy count.

evidence.snippet: The hallmark of ERCC6L2 disease (ED) is a highly penetrant progression from bone marrow failure to erythroid-predominant, TP53-mutated myeloid malignancy with a dismal prognosis.
evidence.explanation: States the progression as the disease's hallmark and gives its molecular and morphological character.

evidence.snippet: Of note, in 7/10 patients progressing to MDS/AML, TP53 mutated clones were described, whereas no such alterations were reported in patients without disease progression.
evidence.explanation: The TP53 association is not merely correlative in this cohort: the clones appear in progressors and in none of the non-progressors.

steps/14.description: The two are curated as one phenotype because the literature reports them as a single progression endpoint and gives a combined denominator. Roughly a third of the pooled cohort reaches it.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic germ line excision repair cross-complementing 6 like 2 (ERCC6L2) variants strongly predispose to bone marrow failure (BMF) and myeloid malignancies, characterized by somatic TP53-mutated clones and erythroid predominance.
evidence.explanation: The malignancy type and its molecular signature are stated for the cohort.

steps/15.description: Erythroid-predominant, with TP53 mutations. Pure or acute erythroid leukaemia is a recognised presentation.

evidence.snippet: All patients displayed bone marrow failure, learning or developmental delay and microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Universal in this six-patient series.

evidence.snippet: Our patients, both homozygous for this variant, as well as the brother of one of them with the same genotype, did not exhibit microcephaly, developmental delay, or dysmorphic features.
evidence.explanation: Three individuals with the same genotype and none of the neurodevelopmental features. Cited as REFUTE against the claim, implied by the disease name, that developmental delay is a required feature.

evidence.snippet: Developmental delay and/or learning difficulties were also described in 6 patients and concurrent microcephaly was present in 5 patients
evidence.explanation: Six affected individuals in a pooled cohort of 31, which is 19% and maps to the OCCASIONAL band rather than FREQUENT.

steps/16.description: Present in all six patients of the 2018 series, but that series is not representative: across the pooled 31-patient literature the combined microcephaly/developmental-delay figure is 6/31, and three individuals in one family had the same genotype with none of these features. The disease name overstates this.

evidence.snippet: Regarding neurological features, 6/31 patients presented microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: The pooled figure, 6 of 31, is 19% and maps to OCCASIONAL. This supersedes the six-patient series below, in which it was universal.

evidence.snippet: All patients displayed bone marrow failure, learning or developmental delay and microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Universal in the six-patient series that defined the phenotype, which is why the early literature reads as though it were obligatory.

evidence.snippet: Our patient was unique in displaying features of cerebellar disease, including ataxia and dysmetria as well as an interval deterioration of the corpus callosum and generalized volume loss on MRI.
evidence.explanation: Described by the authors as unique to their patient, which is the basis for the VERY_RARE band.

steps/18.description: Ataxia and dysmetria with interval deterioration of the corpus callosum and generalised volume loss on MRI, reported in one patient.

evidence.snippet: Another unique feature of our patient was retinal dystrophy with macular involvement.
evidence.explanation: Reported once and described as unique.

evidence.snippet: Patients' LCLs fail to terminate transcript elongation accurately upon DNA damage and display a significant increase in nuclear DNA-RNA hybrids (R loops).
evidence.explanation: Both halves of the mechanism are measured in patient-derived cells.

edges/2.description: ERCC6L2 occupies gene bodies with RNA Pol II and DNA-PK; without it, transcript elongation is not terminated correctly after DNA damage and DNA-RNA hybrids accumulate.

evidence.snippet: All patients displayed bone marrow failure, learning or developmental delay and microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the neurodevelopmental features co-segregate with the marrow phenotype in biallelic ERCC6L2 disease, which is what licenses an edge from the germline lesion. It does not establish a mechanism, which is why the link type is INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES.

edges/3.description:
The neurodevelopmental features are drawn from the germline lesion itself rather than from any step in the haematopoietic chain, because that is what the evidence supports and no more: ERCC6L2 is ubiquitously expressed and the same repair deficiency is present in neural tissue, but no study has shown which step produces the delay, and it is not a consequence of marrow failure. The tissue-level mechanism is genuinely unknown.
Note the penetrance caveat already recorded on the phenotype: the 2018 six-patient series found developmental delay in all of them, but across the pooled 31-patient literature the combined microcephaly/developmental-delay figure is 6 of 31.

evidence.snippet: All patients displayed bone marrow failure, learning or developmental delay and microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Names microcephaly alongside the marrow failure in the same cohort.

edges/4.description: Curated from the germline lesion for the same reason as developmental delay, and reported in the same patients. Whether the small head size reflects reduced neural progenitor output from the same replication stress seen in haematopoietic progenitors is a plausible reading that no cited source demonstrates.

edges/5.description: Reported in a single patient, with interval deterioration on serial MRI. Linked here rather than left detached because it belongs to the same neurological arm, and flagged as VERY_RARE on the phenotype itself so the edge is not read as a general feature.

edges/6.description: The remaining non-haematologic feature, also VERY_RARE. Grouped with the neurological arm on the same basis: a consequence of the ubiquitously expressed germline lesion, with no established route.

evidence.snippet: we demonstrate that Ercc6l2 maintains the competitive fitness of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) by mitigating replication stress.
evidence.explanation: The model attributes the HSPC fitness defect specifically to unmitigated replication stress.

evidence.snippet: Sustained replication stress and DNA damage in Ercc6l2-deficient HSPCs cause p53 pathway activation followed by cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.
evidence.explanation: Same measured sequence, cited on the edge it establishes.

evidence.snippet: Altogether, loss of Ercc6l2 leads to reduced HSPC numbers, bone marrow hypocellularity, and cytopenias.
evidence.explanation: The chain from stem cell loss to marrow hypocellularity to cytopenia is stated as one sequence.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show for the first time that ERCC6L2-deficiency in HSPCs significantly impedes their clonogenic potential and leads to delayed erythroid differentiation.
evidence.explanation: The erythroid-specific delay is measured in human primary HSPCs.

edges/10.description: Erythroid commitment is disproportionately affected, which is the cellular basis of the erythroid predominance seen later in the marrow and in the leukaemias.

evidence.snippet: Most patients presented with trilineage cytopenia
evidence.explanation: Establishes the cytopenia this node contributes to. The source reports trilineage involvement rather than isolating the erythroid lineage, so it supports anaemia being present without attributing it to this node alone — the marrow hypoplasia node below contributes to the same finding.

edges/11.description: The erythroid arrest is what makes anaemia the most consistent cytopenia in this disease, present more often than the thrombocytopenia and neutropenia that arise from generalised marrow hypoplasia.

edges/12.description: Loss of marrow output across lineages. The entry's own phenotype record notes that presentation is often bilineage or isolated rather than trilineage, so this edge asserts the route to cytopenia, not that all three lineages fall together in every patient.

edges/13.description: The megakaryocytic consequence of reduced marrow output.

edges/14.description: The granulocytic consequence of reduced marrow output.

edges/15.description: Generalised marrow hypoplasia contributes to the anaemia alongside the specific erythroid differentiation block above. Both edges are drawn because the sources report trilineage cytopenia with a disproportionate erythroid defect, which is two contributions rather than one.

evidence.snippet: Notably, somatic Trp53 mutations restore cellular fitness of Ercc6l2-deficient HSPCs by abrogating p53 pathway activation and restoring Runx1 and Gata1 expression, thereby correcting the BMF phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The rescue is demonstrated experimentally, and it explains why TP53 clones are selected rather than merely observed.

edges/16.description: Because p53 activation is what removes the mutant stem cells, inactivating p53 restores their fitness. The selection pressure created by the disease selects for the clone that will kill the patient.

evidence.snippet: However, p53 loss fails to normalize replication stress, allowing for the accumulation of DNA damage over time, which increases the likelihood for leukemic transformation.
evidence.explanation: The same sentence names the transformation as the consequence.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic germ line excision repair cross-complementing 6 like 2 (ERCC6L2) variants strongly predispose to bone marrow failure (BMF) and myeloid malignancies, characterized by somatic TP53-mutated clones and erythroid predominance.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the predisposition this node realises, and names both defining features of it — the somatic TP53 clones and the erythroid predominance.

edges/18.description: The clinical diagnosis this node describes. Both are curated as one phenotype because ERCC6L2 disease is reported as a continuum in which the MDS/AML boundary is often not drawn.

edges/19.description: The specific malignancy curated separately from the combined MDS/AML phenotype above, for entries and queries that need AML as its own term.

evidence.snippet: Collectively, these observations identify a distinct bone-marrow-failure syndrome due to mutations in ERCC6L2, a gene implicated in DNA repair and mitochondrial function.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease discovery statement.

genes/0.notes: Nineteen different variants across 35 families, including a Finnish founder allele c.1424delT. Reported variants are truncating and lie at or upstream of the helicase domain.

steps/1.description:
A single SLFN14 allele carries a missense variant. The reported variants cluster tightly: K218E, K219N and V220D lie in three consecutive residues of the AAA domain, and R223W sits four residues further along, so the recurrent lesion is a small patch of the RNA-binding cleft rather than a scatter across the protein.
Later reports have added variants in the C-terminal helicase domain, which is a different part of the protein and appears to act differently; those are noted on the gene entry rather than folded into this node.

evidence.snippet: Compared to SLFN14 WT, expression of mutants is dramatically reduced as a result of post-translational degradation due to partial misfolding of the protein.
